title: Birds: Anatomy, Behavior, and Field Identification
description: An introduction to the biology of birds for learners with no formal background. The course moves from what makes a bird a bird (feathers, skeleton and evolutionary history) through flight, internal anatomy and the senses, to the practical skill of identifying birds by sight and sound. Later chapters cover breeding, migration and the conservation of bird populations. Each chapter pairs reading with practice you can do outdoors or with photographs and recordings.
objectives: Describe the anatomical traits that define birds and explain how they support flight.
Explain the evidence that birds are living dinosaurs.
Identify common birds to species using shape, field marks, behavior, habitat and sound.
Describe how birds court, nest, raise young and migrate.
Interpret bird population data and explain the main threats to birds and the measures that have reversed declines.
Collect and submit a standardized bird survey to a citizen-science project.

preface:
This book is an introduction to the biology of birds for readers who have never studied it formally. It begins with the question that defines the field, what makes a bird a bird, and answers it with anatomy and the fossil record before turning to flight, physiology, identification, song, breeding, migration and conservation. Each chapter rests on the ones before it, so the order matters.

Every section follows the same plan. Read the text, study the figure, work through the example, then attempt the three practice problems before moving on. The chapter quiz checks whether the ideas have settled; the challenge exercises ask you to use them on real birds. Numbers in square brackets point to the sources listed after each section. I have kept to the scholarly literature and standard references so that you can follow any claim back to its evidence.

Ornithology rewards patience and attention more than prior knowledge. A notebook, a field guide and an hour outdoors each week will teach you as much as these pages, and the two together will teach you more than either alone.

title: Game Design: Systems, Mechanics, and Player Experience
description: A course for learners who have played games critically and perhaps made small prototypes, and now want the working methods of professional designers. It treats a game as a system of rules that produces player experience, and teaches the tools designers use to shape that system: core loops, feedback, economies, difficulty curves, level layout and playtesting. Every chapter ends with a design exercise that you can complete on paper or in a simple prototype.

Basic arithmetic and spreadsheets; no programming required

preface:
This book is for people who have played a lot of games, maybe built a prototype or two, and now want to work the way designers in studios work. Each chapter gives you one set of tools, shows it at work in games you probably know (*Tetris*, *Super Mario Bros.*, *Slay the Spire*), and then asks you to use it on a design of your own.

That design is a small card game you start in Chapter 1 and improve in every chapter after it. Paper, index cards and a spreadsheet are all you need. Paper is faster than code for learning design, because you can change a rule in ten seconds and play again.

Expect your first versions to be bad; everyone's are. The real skill this book teaches is noticing why a design is not working and changing it, which is why playtesting runs through every chapter and gets one of its own.

title: Outer Space from the Ground Up
description: A first look at space for someone starting from zero. The course begins with what you can see from your own backyard and works outward: the Moon and planets, the Sun, the stars, and the galaxies beyond. Distances and sizes are built up with everyday comparisons before any numbers are introduced. You will finish able to find major objects in the night sky and explain how astronomers know what they know.

preface:
This book is about space, and it starts right where you are standing. You do not need to know anything yet. You only need to look up.

We begin with what your own eyes can see (the Sun, the Moon, the planets and the stars) and go a little farther out in each chapter, past the planets, out to other stars and on to other galaxies. To make the huge distances feel real, we will build one scale model and keep extending it: in it, the Sun is a ball the size of a bowling ball and Earth is a peppercorn across a football field.

You will also keep a sky diary, a few lines about what you see on clear nights. Every fact in this book is checked, and every big claim comes with the story of how someone found it out.

title: Energy Systems: Conversion, Storage, and the Electric Grid
department: Department of Mechanical and Electrical Engineering
description: An upper-division treatment of how societies convert, store, move and use energy. The course applies thermodynamics, electrical engineering and economics to real systems: thermal power plants, wind and solar generation, batteries and other storage, and the operation of the power grid. Students work with quantitative models throughout, including efficiency limits, capacity factors, levelized cost and dispatch. The final chapter combines these tools to evaluate decarbonization pathways.
prerequisites: Single-variable calculus
Introductory physics (mechanics and electricity)
Basic thermodynamics or chemistry recommended
objectives: Apply the first and second laws of thermodynamics to compute efficiency limits of heat engines and real power cycles.
Analyze AC power, phasors, transmission losses and power factor in grid components.
Estimate output and capacity factor of wind and solar installations from resource data.

Compute levelized cost of energy and explain its limits as a comparison tool.
Model merit-order dispatch and explain how variable renewables change grid operation.

preface:
Every energy system is a chain of conversions, and every link in the chain loses something. This book traces those chains with numbers: from fuel, wind or sunlight, through engines, turbines and semiconductors, onto a grid that must match supply and demand second by second, and into the motors, lights and heat pumps where energy finally does useful work.

The tools are thermodynamics, circuit theory and a little economics. If you are comfortable with calculus and introductory physics, you have what you need. Expect to compute: Carnot limits, line losses, capacity factors, levelized costs. We will follow one kilowatt-hour from source to socket, and return again and again to a gas plant, a wind farm and a real day on a large grid.

The last chapter puts the pieces together on the question that now drives the field, how to run an electric system with far less carbon, so that you can read a decarbonization study and say which of its assumptions matter.

topic: Ancient aliens: the claims and the archaeological evidence
title: Ancient Aliens: The Claims, the Evidence, and the People Who Really Built the Ancient World
description: An introduction to the ancient-astronaut idea for curious readers with no background in archaeology. The book takes the famous claims seriously enough to test them: where the idea came from, what is said about Giza, the Nazca lines, Puma Punku, the moai of Rapa Nui, Palenque and Baalbek, and what excavation, dating and experiment have actually found at each site. It does not teach that aliens built these places, because the evidence shows, site by site, that people did; instead it names those people and shows how they did it. Along the way you learn how archaeologists date and read evidence, and a fair method for weighing any extraordinary claim.
objectives: Trace the ancient-astronaut idea from its earlier roots through Erich von Däniken's 1968 bestseller to modern television, and state its core claims fairly.
Explain how archaeologists date a site and read its evidence, using context, stratigraphy, radiocarbon dating, inscriptions and tool marks.
For Giza, the Nazca lines, Puma Punku, Baalbek, the moai and the Palenque tomb lid, state the ancient-astronaut claim and summarize the evidence for who made each and how.
Describe how experimental archaeology tests ancient methods, using the moai-walking experiment and the 3D-printed reconstruction of Puma Punku as examples.
Apply a six-question checklist (claim, source, burden of proof, testability, simplest sufficient explanation, expert evidence) to a claim you have not seen before.
Explain how ancient-astronaut claims take credit away from real ancient peoples, and why that matters to their descendants.
Follow a claim about the ancient past back to an excavation report, museum record or peer-reviewed study.

preface:
If you have ever watched a program about ancient aliens and wondered whether there might be something to it, this book is for you. Wondering is the right instinct. The Great Pyramid, the Nazca lines and the stones of Puma Punku are astonishing, and anyone who sees them should ask how they were made. This book asks that question seriously, site by site, and follows the evidence wherever it leads.

Here is how it works. Each chapter states a famous claim fairly, in the words of the people who make it, and then shows what archaeologists have found: quarries and tool marks, workers' towns, dated layers, inscriptions and experiments. Chapter 2 gives you the toolkit archaeologists use to date things and read evidence, and you will use it in every chapter after. You will also keep claim cards, one for each claim you meet: what is said, who said it first, what the evidence shows, and your verdict.

I will tell you now where the evidence leads, so there are no tricks. At every site in this book, people built what we see, and we know a great deal about who they were and how they did it. That is the best part of the story. The crews who hauled limestone for King Khufu, the Nazca who drew on the desert, the stonemasons of Tiwanaku and the carvers of Rapa Nui deserve the credit. By the last page you will be able to give it to them, and to weigh any extraordinary claim fairly.

bible.teacher: Dr. Professor teaches this book as a field archaeologist who has heard every ancient-astronaut claim and still enjoys them: from excavation reports, quarries, tool marks, dated layers, inscriptions and experiments, and from the claimants' own books, quoted fairly before they are tested.
bible.promise: By the last page you will be able to take any claim about the ancient past, find out where it came from, weigh the evidence fairly, and tell the true story of who built the world's great monuments.
threads: Claim, then evidence: every chapter states the claim fairly, as its proponents put it, before testing it.

How we know: The archaeologist's toolkit, shared by ARC 101, EGY 101 and ANE 101: context (where a thing was found and with what), stratigraphy (lower layers are older), dating methods that check each other (radiocarbon, tree rings, inscriptions and king lists, styles of pottery and objects), materials analysis, written texts read in the original, and experimental archaeology.
Name the builders: every site is credited to the people who made it, with how they did it.
Curiosity is the point: a mystery is an invitation to look harder, and the real answers are more remarkable than the claims.

Name the builders: the Egyptians of Khufu's reign, the Nazca, the people of Tiwanaku, the Rapa Nui, the Maya of Palenque, the Romans at Baalbek; not 'the ancients'.
Say 'ancient-astronaut claim' or 'idea', not 'theory', which in science means a well-tested explanation.
Dates as BC and AD, with 'about' for approximate dates; give the dating method behind any key date. Metric units with a familiar comparison.
Cross-reference the companion books by code: ANE 101 (Sumer and Sitchin's Anunnaki) and EGY 101 (Egyptian faience and glass) share this book's dating and evidence methods.

bible.care: The reader asked for 'Ancient Aliens'. This book does not teach that aliens visited or built anything in the ancient world, because no evidence supports it and abundant evidence shows that people built every site discussed. It teaches the claims as claims: stated fairly, traced to their sources, and tested against excavation, dating and experiment. Say so plainly and kindly; never mock the reader for being curious, and criticize arguments rather than the people who make or believe them. Where archaeologists genuinely disagree (how the moai were moved, which ramps built the Great Pyramid, what the Nazca lines were for), present the debate honestly as open questions about how people did it, not whether they did. Treat the claims' habit of denying credit to non-European peoples plainly and with respect for their descendants. Von Däniken's and Sitchin's books are quoted as the sources of the claims, never cited as evidence.

title: Ancient Egyptian Glass: From the Core-Formed Vessel to the Blowpipe
department: Department of Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations, Egyptology Program
description: An introduction to how the ancient Egyptians made faience and glass, for readers with no background in archaeology or chemistry. It is not a book about Egyptian glassblowing, because for most of Egyptian history nobody blew glass: Egyptians made glazed faience from Predynastic times and glass vessels from the New Kingdom (from the 15th century BC) by winding hot glass around a removable core or casting it in molds. Glassblowing was invented in the Syro-Palestinian region in the first century BC, spread under Rome, and only then made Roman Egypt, with Alexandria, a major glass center. The book follows that true story through real objects, excavated workshops, a Bronze Age shipwreck and the chemistry that tells where glass was made.
objectives: Explain what glass and Egyptian faience are made of and how they differ.
Describe step by step how core-formed and cast glass vessels were made in New Kingdom Egypt.

Explain how chemical analysis of the Uluburun glass ingots is used to trace Late Bronze Age glass trade, and why the results are debated.

preface:
This book began with a question about Egyptian glassblowing, and the honest answer is the most interesting thing in it. For almost all of ancient Egyptian history, nobody anywhere blew glass. Egyptian craftsmen made shining blue faience for thousands of years, and from the reign of Thutmose III, in the 15th century BC, they made glass vessels by winding hot glass around a core or shaping it in molds. The blowpipe was invented much later, in the first century BC, on the eastern shore of the Mediterranean. Only after it reached Egypt under Roman rule did Alexandria become one of the great glass cities of the Roman world.

The five chapters follow that story in order: faience, the first glass vessels, the royal workshops at Amarna and Qantir, a Bronze Age shipwreck full of glass ingots, and finally the blowpipe. In each one you will look at real objects and real workshops, and learn how archaeologists date them and how chemistry can tell where a piece of glass was made. These are the same methods used in our books on ancient-astronaut claims (ARC 101) and on Sumer (ANE 101), so the three can be read together.

You do not need any chemistry, only curiosity and a museum website or two, because the challenges ask you to look closely at real objects. Please do not try to melt or work glass at home; it needs furnace heat and training. Looking closely is safe, and it will teach you more.

bible.teacher: Dr. Professor teaches this book as an archaeological scientist would: from excavated workshops, dated objects in museum collections, chemical analyses and craft reconstruction, using the same dating and evidence methods as ARC 101 and ANE 101.
bible.promise: By the last page you will be able to look at a piece of ancient Egyptian faience or glass, say how and roughly when it was made, and explain why the blowpipe came so late in Egypt's story.
threads: Get the sequence right: faience, then core-formed and cast glass, then blowing, and what changed at each step.
Technique leaves traces: how an object was made can be read from its shape, surface and chemistry.

How we know: The archaeologist's toolkit, shared by ARC 101, EGY 101 and ANE 101: context (where a thing was found and with what), stratigraphy (lower layers are older), dating methods that check each other (radiocarbon, tree rings, inscriptions and king lists, styles of pottery and objects), materials analysis, written texts read in the original, and experimental archaeology.
Glass as artificial precious stone: color, value and display from faience to Roman tableware.

runningExamples.name: The Menkheperre cup
runningExamples.use: The fragmentary blue glass cup naming Thutmose III from the tomb of his foreign wives: the anchor for dating the first Egyptian glass vessels.

runningExamples.name: A core-formed cosmetic jar
runningExamples.use: A typical New Kingdom vessel with zigzag trails, followed through how it was made, used, dated and analyzed.

runningExamples.name: Amarna site O45.1
runningExamples.use: The workshop where glass, faience and pigment were made side by side (Chapters 3 and 4).

runningExamples.name: The Uluburun glass ingots
runningExamples.use: Raw glass in transit: trade, chemical fingerprinting and an open scholarly debate.

runningExamples.name: A Roman blown bottle from Egypt
runningExamples.use: The endpoint: what the blowpipe changed, set beside the core-formed jar.

conventions: Use 'core-formed', 'cast', 'free-blown' and 'mold-blown' precisely; never call pre-Roman Egyptian glass 'blown'.
Dates as BC and AD with 'about' for approximate dates; give the evidence behind each key date (a royal name, a dated context, an analysis).
Kings by their usual Egyptological names (Thutmose III, Akhenaten, Ramesses II), with reign dates from the canon at first mention.
Metric units and degrees Celsius, each with a familiar comparison.
Cross-reference ARC 101 Chapter 2 and ANE 101 Chapter 1 for the shared dating and evidence methods.

canon.role: A short, beginner-friendly overview of faience and glass technology, pitched at this book's level.

canon.cite: Shortland, A. (2012). Lapis lazuli from the kiln: Glass and glassmaking in the Late Bronze Age (Studies in Archaeological Sciences 2). Leuven University Press.
canon.role: The origins, golden age, workshops, trade and decline of Late Bronze Age glass (Chapters 2 to 4).

canon.cite: Rehren, T., & Pusch, E. B. (2005). Late Bronze Age glass production at Qantir-Piramesses, Egypt. Science, 308(5729), 1756-1758.
canon.role: Primary research: crucibles showing glass made from raw materials in Egypt (Chapter 3).

canon.role: Primary research: chemical evidence for the origin of the Uluburun ingots (Chapter 4).

canon.cite: Stern, E. M. (1999). Roman glassblowing in a cultural context. American Journal of Archaeology, 103, 441–484.
canon.role: The invention and spread of glassblowing and what it changed (Chapter 5).

canon.cite: Corning Museum of Glass. (n.d.). Collection and online resources on ancient glass. https://www.cmog.org
canon.role: Museum reference (website): dated core-formed and Roman blown vessels, and accessible accounts of core-forming and glassblowing.

bible.care: The reader asked about 'Ancient Egyptian glass blowing'. The book says plainly, in the description, the preface, Chapter 2 and Chapter 5, that glassblowing was not practiced in pharaonic Egypt: Egyptians made faience from Predynastic times and glass vessels by core-forming and casting from the New Kingdom, while the blowpipe was invented in the Syro-Palestinian region in the first century BC and reached Egypt under Roman rule. Treat this as correcting a very common assumption, not as the reader's mistake. Where specialists disagree (where glass was first made, how many stages glassmaking took at Amarna and Qantir, where the Uluburun ingots were made), present each view with its evidence. Safety: molten glass, furnaces and glass dust and shards are dangerous. Describe ancient methods, but never ask the reader to melt, blow or grind glass; challenges use drawings, museum collections and data.

title: Breakfast Cooking: Eggs, Pancakes, Porridge and the Morning Cup
description: A hands-on first cooking course built around the meal most people cook for themselves. Five chapters cover eggs, pancakes and waffles, bacon and sausage, oats and other grains, and coffee and tea, and every chapter is a cook-along: you cook while you read. Each technique comes with the short reason it works and the safety rule that goes with it, including the USDA rules for eggs and meat. For the full science, each chapter points to the matching chapter of its companion book, Food Science (FDS 201).
prerequisites: No cooking experience needed.
Equipment: a stove, a nonstick or well-seasoned frying pan, a saucepan, a kitchen scale or measuring cups, and an instant-read food thermometer.
objectives: Cook eggs six ways (boiled, poached, fried, scrambled, as an omelet and baked) and control their texture with temperature and time.
Follow the USDA egg rules: keep eggs refrigerated, cook them until yolks and whites are firm, cook egg dishes to 160°F (71°C), and use pasteurized eggs for runny yolks or raw-egg dishes.
Make pancakes and waffles from scratch and explain how baking soda, baking powder, eggs and steam make them rise.
Cook bacon and sausage to a browned, safe finish, keeping raw meat apart from ready-to-eat food and cooking fresh pork or beef sausage to 160°F (71°C) and poultry sausage to 165°F (74°C).
Cook porridge from rolled and steel-cut oats and other grains, adjusting liquid and time to the grain.
Brew coffee and tea by controlling ratio, grind or leaf, water temperature and time, and taste the effect of each change.
Plan and cook a complete breakfast for four, timing each part to be ready together.

chapters.title: Eggs Every Way
chapters.summary: Boiled, poached, fried, scrambled, omelets and baked eggs, with the protein science behind each texture and the USDA rules: keep eggs refrigerated at 40°F (4°C) or below, cook them until yolks and whites are firm, cook egg dishes to 160°F (71°C), and use pasteurized eggs for runny yolks.
chapters.challenge: Cook-along: boil six pasteurized eggs for six different times, line them up from runny to firm and explain each texture by the proteins that have set, then scramble eggs low and slow and hot and fast and describe the difference.

sections.title: Inside an egg
sections.summary: Shell, white and yolk, the proteins in each, and how to buy, store and crack eggs safely.

sections.title: Boiled and poached
sections.summary: Cooking eggs in water: timing a boiled egg, making it easy to peel, and keeping a poached egg together.

sections.title: Fried, scrambled, omelets and frittatas
sections.summary: Cooking eggs in a pan: heat level, fat, and why low heat and steady stirring make creamy curds.

sections.title: Egg safety
sections.summary: Salmonella, the USDA handling rules, the 160°F (71°C) rule for egg dishes, and pasteurized in-shell eggs for anything served runny or raw.

chapters.title: Pancakes, Waffles and Leavening
chapters.summary: How batters work and what makes them rise: gluten, baking soda with an acid, double-acting baking powder, steam and beaten eggs.
chapters.challenge: Cook-along: make one batch of buttermilk pancake batter, cook some at once and some after a 20-minute rest, then make a small batch with the baking soda left out, and explain the differences you see and taste.

sections.title: What is in a batter
sections.summary: Flour, liquid, eggs, fat and sugar, and the job each one does.

sections.title: Chemical leavening
sections.summary: Baking soda needs an acid, baking powder carries its own, and both make bubbles of carbon dioxide.

sections.title: Mixing and resting
sections.summary: Why a lumpy batter makes tender pancakes and an overmixed one makes tough ones.

sections.title: Griddle and waffle iron
sections.summary: Heat level, why the first pancake often fails, and what makes a waffle crisp outside and soft inside.

chapters.title: Bacon, Sausage and the Maillard Reaction
chapters.summary: Rendering fat and browning meat, with the safety rules: keep raw meat and its juices away from ready-to-eat food, and cook fresh pork or beef sausage to 160°F (71°C) and poultry sausage to 165°F (74°C), checked with a thermometer.
chapters.challenge: Cook-along: cook bacon three ways (started in a cold pan, in a hot pan and in the oven) and compare fat rendering, crispness and browning, then cook sausage patties and check each one with a thermometer.

sections.title: Cured and fresh meats
sections.summary: What bacon, ham and sausage are, and how curing changes meat.

sections.title: Rendering fat
sections.summary: Why bacon started in a cold pan or in the oven melts its fat before the meat browns.

sections.title: The Maillard reaction at the stove
sections.summary: The browning reaction behind bacon, sausage and toast, and why a dry, hot surface browns best.

sections.title: Cooking meat safely
sections.summary: Keeping raw meat separate, washing hands and boards, using a thermometer, and the safe temperatures for sausage.

chapters.title: Oats, Porridge and Grains
chapters.summary: How rolled, steel-cut and whole oats and other grains take up water and soften, and how to make porridge creamy or chewy, plus overnight oats, grits and rice porridge.
chapters.challenge: Cook-along: cook rolled oats and steel-cut oats side by side, measuring the water and time each needs, then make a jar of overnight oats and compare all three textures.

sections.title: What a grain is
sections.summary: Bran, germ and endosperm, and how oats are cut, rolled and steamed into different products.

sections.title: Starch and water
sections.summary: How starch granules swell and leak starch to make porridge creamy.

sections.title: Porridge methods
sections.summary: Stovetop, overnight and baked oats, with ratios and times for each kind of oat.

sections.title: Beyond oats
sections.summary: Grits, polenta, rice porridge and homemade granola.

chapters.title: Coffee and Tea
chapters.summary: Brewing as extraction: how grind, ratio, water temperature and time draw flavor out of coffee and tea, starting from the Specialty Coffee Association's widely used ratio of about 55 grams of coffee per liter of water.
chapters.challenge: Cook-along: brew the same coffee at three grind sizes (or the same tea for three steeping times), taste each, describe the change from sour through balanced to bitter, then cook and serve the whole Saturday breakfast.

sections.title: Extraction
sections.summary: What dissolves from coffee and tea into hot water, in what order, and how that changes the taste.

sections.title: Brewing coffee
sections.summary: Ratio, grind size, water temperature and contact time in pour-over, French press, drip and espresso.

sections.title: Brewing tea
sections.summary: Black, green, oolong and white teas from one plant, and how leaf, water temperature and steeping time shape the cup.

sections.title: The finished cup
sections.summary: How water, milk and sugar change the drink, and how much caffeine coffee and tea contain.

preface:
This is a cooking book you use at the stove. Every chapter is a cook-along: read a little, cook a little, taste, and read on. Breakfast is the right place to start, because it is quick, cheap and made every day, so you get to practice every morning. By the end you will cook eggs exactly the way you like them, make pancakes from scratch, cook bacon and sausage well and safely, make a good bowl of porridge, and brew coffee or tea you enjoy.

Each technique comes with a short reason. Eggs set because their proteins unfold and link together as they heat. Pancakes rise because baking soda and an acid make bubbles of gas. Bacon browns because of the Maillard reaction. Knowing the reason lets you fix a dish instead of starting over. When you want the whole story, each chapter points to the chapter of the companion book, Food Science, that explains it in depth.

Some rules here are not about taste. Eggs and raw meat can carry bacteria that make people sick, so you will use a thermometer and follow the USDA safe temperatures, and I will give you each one plainly where it applies. You will need a frying pan, a saucepan, a scale or measuring cups, and that thermometer. Keep a few notes on what you cooked and how it turned out. By the last chapter you will cook a whole breakfast for four and have it all ready at the same time.

bible.teacher: Dr. Professor teaches this book as a cook standing beside you at the stove: show the technique, give the reason in a sentence or two, state the safety rule plainly, then hand you the pan. Reasons come from McGee and the companion Food Science book, tested technique from López-Alt and Nosrat, and safety rules from USDA FSIS.
bible.promise: By the last page you will cook a whole breakfast (eggs, pancakes, bacon or sausage, porridge, and coffee or tea) confidently, safely and to your own taste, and know why each step works.
threads: Cook along: every section ends at the stove with something to make, look at and taste.
Heat and time control texture: the same egg, batter or grain changes completely with a few degrees or a few minutes.
Know the reason: one or two sentences of science per technique, with a pointer to Food Science (FDS 201) for the full story.
Safety rules are stated plainly and never skipped: refrigeration, keeping raw meat separate, and safe temperatures checked with a thermometer.

runningExamples.name: The Saturday breakfast
runningExamples.use: A full breakfast for four built up one chapter at a time and cooked all together at the end of Chapter 5, so the reader learns timing as well as technique.

runningExamples.name: The egg
runningExamples.use: The ingredient in every chapter's story: on its own (Ch 1), in the batter (Ch 2), beside the bacon (Ch 3), and on top of a savory porridge (Ch 4).

runningExamples.name: The breakfast notebook
runningExamples.use: A short record of each cook-along: what you changed, what happened, and what you will do next time.

conventions: Every cook-along lists equipment, ingredients by weight and by volume, numbered steps, and what to look, listen and smell for.
Give temperatures in °F and °C, quoting USDA safety temperatures exactly as USDA states them (160°F, 71°C; 165°F, 74°C).
Point to the companion book by chapter number and title when the science is fuller there ("see Food Science, Chapter 2, Proteins").
Plain words and short steps; define any technical term the first time it appears.
Present practitioner advice (Nosrat, López-Alt) as a cook's tested experience, and science (McGee, Food Science) as mechanism.

canon.role: The science of eggs, batters, cured meats, grains, coffee and tea; the source for each short 'why'.

canon.cite: López-Alt, J. K. (2015). The food lab: Better home cooking through science. W. W. Norton.
canon.role: Practitioner cookbook: tested breakfast techniques (eggs, pancakes, bacon) and side-by-side kitchen tests that the cook-alongs adapt.

canon.cite: Nosrat, S. (2017). Salt, fat, acid, heat: Mastering the elements of good cooking. Simon & Schuster.
canon.role: Practitioner book (a chef's teaching, not a science text): how salt, fat, acid and heat shape flavor and texture; used for seasoning and cooking judgment, not for scientific claims.

canon.cite: U.S. Department of Agriculture, Food Safety and Inspection Service. (n.d.). Safe minimum internal temperature chart. https://www.fsis.usda.gov/food-safety/safe-food-handling-and-preparation/food-safety-basics/safe-temperature-chart
canon.role: Safe minimum internal temperatures quoted exactly: 160°F for egg dishes and for ground meat, including fresh pork or beef sausage; 165°F for poultry, including poultry sausage; raw eggs cooked until yolk and white are firm.

canon.cite: U.S. Department of Agriculture, Food Safety and Inspection Service. (n.d.). Shell eggs from farm to table. https://www.fsis.usda.gov
canon.role: Egg handling: keep eggs refrigerated, cook them until the yolks are firm, avoid raw or undercooked eggs (especially for infants, young children, older adults, pregnant women and people with weakened immune systems), and use pasteurized in-shell eggs for dishes served without cooking.

canon.cite: U.S. Department of Agriculture, Food Safety and Inspection Service. (n.d.). "Danger zone" (40°F - 140°F). https://www.fsis.usda.gov
canon.role: The danger zone and the 2-hour rule (1 hour above 90°F) for leftovers and for food left out on a breakfast table.

bible.care: Safety rules are stated plainly in the chapters where they apply. Eggs: keep them in a refrigerator at 40°F (4°C) or below, cook them until yolks and whites are firm, and cook egg dishes such as frittatas and quiches to 160°F (71°C). For runny yolks, soft scrambles or anything made with raw egg, use pasteurized in-shell eggs, which USDA says may be used safely without cooking. Infants, young children, older adults, pregnant women and people with weakened immune systems should not eat raw or undercooked eggs. Meat: keep raw meat and its juices away from ready-to-eat food, wash hands, boards and tools after handling it, and cook fresh pork or beef sausage to 160°F (71°C) and poultry sausage to 165°F (74°C), checked with a thermometer. Leftovers go into the refrigerator within 2 hours, or 1 hour when it is above 90°F (32°C). Hot fat, boiling water and hot drinks burn, so every cook-along says how to handle them safely. Coffee and tea brewing figures (such as the Specialty Coffee Association's ratio) are quality guidelines, not safety rules, and are presented as starting points to adjust by taste.

title: Catholicism and the Bible: Scripture, Creed, Sacraments and Prayer
department: Department of Theology and Religious Studies
description: A first course for anyone who wants to understand what the Catholic Church believes and how it reads the Bible, whether you are Catholic, from another tradition, or of no religion. It explains the Bible's books and why the Catholic Bible has 73 of them, how Catholics read Scripture together with Tradition and the Church's teaching office, and then the Creed, the sacraments, the moral life and prayer, always in the Church's own words from the Catechism and the Second Vatican Council. Throughout, it marks clearly what the Church teaches as a matter of faith and what historians and biblical scholars argue from evidence. It explains belief without asking you to share it.
prerequisites: No prior knowledge of the Bible, Christianity or theology
A Catholic Bible, such as the New American Bible, Revised Edition (NABRE), in print or free online
objectives: Find any passage in a Catholic Bible by book, chapter and verse, and name the main sections and kinds of writing in each Testament.
Explain why Catholic Bibles contain 73 books, name the deuterocanonical books, and distinguish the Church's teaching on the canon from historians' account of how it formed.
Explain how the Church understands revelation, Scripture, Tradition and the Magisterium, using Dei Verbum.
Identify the literal sense and the three spiritual senses of Scripture in a given passage.
Summarize each article of the Nicene Creed and what the Church teaches about it, citing the Catechism.
Name the seven sacraments, describe the shape of the Mass, and explain the seasons of the liturgical year.
State the main principles of Catholic moral and social teaching and describe the main forms of Catholic prayer.
For any claim in the book, say whether it is Church teaching, theological opinion or a finding of historical scholarship.

chapters.title: What the Bible Is
chapters.summary: A library of books written over many centuries, and how the Catholic Bible came to have 73 of them.
chapters.challenge: Look up and read one short passage from each of four kinds of writing (law, history, prophecy and wisdom), recording each reference and saying what kind of writing it is and how you can tell.

sections.title: A library in two testaments

sections.title: How the canon formed: history and teaching

sections.title: Translations and Catholic Bibles
sections.summary: From Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek into English, and what makes an edition a Catholic one.

chapters.title: How Catholics Read Scripture
chapters.summary: Revelation, Scripture and Tradition, the Church's teaching office, and the senses of Scripture.

sections.title: Revelation, Scripture and Tradition
sections.summary: Dei Verbum's teaching that God's word comes through Scripture and Tradition together, and the role of the Magisterium.

sections.title: Inspiration and truth
sections.summary: What the Church means by inspiration, and Dei Verbum 11 on the truth Scripture teaches 'for the sake of salvation'.

sections.title: The four senses of Scripture
sections.summary: The literal sense and the allegorical, moral and anagogical senses (Catechism 115 to 119).

sections.title: Methods old and new

chapters.title: The Old Testament
chapters.summary: The story, law, prophecy, poetry and wisdom of Israel, read for what it says and for how the Church receives it.

sections.title: Beginnings: Genesis and the Pentateuch
sections.summary: Creation, the ancestors of Israel, the Exodus and the covenant at Sinai, and how scholars think the first five books were composed.

sections.title: Land, kings and exile
sections.summary: The historical books from Joshua to the return from Babylon, and what archaeology adds.

sections.title: Prophets, psalms and wisdom
sections.summary: Isaiah, Jeremiah and the other prophets, the Psalms, and the wisdom books, including the deuterocanonical Wisdom and Sirach.

sections.title: The Old Testament in the Church
sections.summary: Its lasting value, the reading of types and figures, and respect for Jewish reading of the same Scriptures.

chapters.title: The New Testament
chapters.summary: Gospels, Acts, letters and Revelation: what they contain and how they came to be written.

sections.title: Acts and the letters of Paul

chapters.title: The Creed

sections.title: What a creed is
sections.summary: The Apostles' Creed and the Nicene Creed, and where they came from.

sections.title: God, creation and the Trinity
sections.summary: One God in three Persons, creation, and how the Church reads Genesis 1 to 3 (Catechism 337 and 390).

sections.title: Jesus Christ
sections.summary: The Incarnation, the Passion, the Resurrection and the Ascension as the Church professes them.

sections.title: The Spirit, the Church and the life to come

chapters.title: Liturgy and the Seven Sacraments
chapters.summary: How the Church worships, and the seven sacraments that mark a Catholic life.
chapters.challenge: Attend or watch a Sunday Mass, or read its order in a missal, and map each part onto this chapter's outline, noting every place where Scripture is read or quoted.

sections.title: Liturgy and the shape of the Mass
sections.summary: The Liturgy of the Word and the Liturgy of the Eucharist, and what the Church teaches about the Eucharist.

sections.title: Sacraments of initiation
sections.summary: Baptism, Confirmation and the Eucharist, and the scriptural roots the Church sees in each.

sections.title: Sacraments of healing
sections.summary: Penance (Reconciliation) and the Anointing of the Sick.

sections.title: Sacraments at the service of communion
sections.summary: Holy Orders and Matrimony.

preface:
This book explains what the Catholic Church believes and how it reads the Bible, for anyone who wants to understand it: Catholics who want to know their faith better, Christians from other churches, and readers of any religion or none. You do not need to know anything about the Bible yet. You only need a Catholic Bible to hand, or the free online text, so that you can look things up as we go.

The first half is about the Bible itself: what it is, which books are in it and why, how Catholics read it, and what is in the Old and New Testaments. The second half follows the four parts of the Catechism of the Catholic Church: what Catholics believe (the Creed), how they worship (the liturgy and sacraments), how they are called to live (the moral life), and how they pray. Whenever I write 'the Church teaches', I give you the paragraph of the Catechism or the Council document, so you can read it for yourself.

I will also tell you which kind of claim you are reading. 'The Church teaches that Scripture is inspired by God' is a statement of faith. 'Most scholars date Mark's Gospel to around the year 70' is a judgment of historical scholarship. Both are worth knowing, and the Church itself asks for both kinds of study, but they are different things, and you will understand Catholicism far better if you keep them apart.

A few passages travel with us through the whole book: the creation stories of Genesis, the Exodus and the Passover, the Lord's Prayer and the parable of the Good Samaritan. By the end you will have read each of them in several ways and seen how one text can carry history, teaching, worship and prayer at once.

bible.teacher: Dr. Professor teaches this book as a careful scholar of Catholic theology and of the Bible would: explaining Catholic belief from the Church's own sources (the Catechism, the documents of the Second Vatican Council, the Pontifical Biblical Commission) and from the biblical text, and reporting historical and critical scholarship (Raymond Brown, Lawrence Boadt) as scholarship, always saying which is which.
bible.promise: By the last page you will be able to find your way around a Catholic Bible, explain the Creed, sacraments, moral teaching and prayer of the Catholic Church in its own terms, and tell Church teaching apart from historical scholarship.
threads: Scripture, Tradition and the Magisterium work together in Catholic belief (Dei Verbum 10); every chapter shows how.
Every claim is labeled: Church teaching (with a Catechism or council reference), theological opinion, or historical scholarship.
The Bible is heard in the Church's worship: each chapter shows where its passages are read at Mass or prayed.
The Old and New Testaments shed light on each other, in the saying of Augustine quoted in Dei Verbum 16.

runningExamples.name: Genesis 1 to 3
runningExamples.use: The creation stories and the fall: literary forms and inspiration (Chapter 2), the Pentateuch (Chapter 3), and creation and original sin in the Creed (Chapter 5), with the Church's own reading (Catechism 337, 390).

runningExamples.name: The Exodus and the Passover (Exodus 12 to 15)
runningExamples.use: The model passage for the four senses of Scripture, for history and archaeology set beside teaching, and for Baptism, the Eucharist and the Easter Vigil.

runningExamples.name: The Lord's Prayer (Matthew 6:9-13; Luke 11:2-4)
runningExamples.use: Two Gospel versions for the synoptic question (Chapter 4), the prayer said at every Mass, and the Catechism's closing commentary (Chapter 8).

runningExamples.name: The Good Samaritan (Luke 10:25-37)
runningExamples.use: A parable read literally and, by Church Fathers such as Augustine, allegorically; the anchor for moral and social teaching in Chapter 7.

conventions: Quote the Bible from the NABRE; give references as book chapter:verse (Exodus 14:21-22), with Catholic book names and the NABRE's psalm numbering.
Cite the Catechism by paragraph number (CCC 115-119) and council documents by name and section (Dei Verbum 12).
Introduce teaching with 'the Church teaches' or 'Catholics believe', and scholarship with 'most scholars', 'many historians' or a named scholar; never blur the two.
Use the Church's own terms (Eucharist, Magisterium, deuterocanonical) and define each at first use; note other Christians' terms where they differ (for example, Apocrypha).
Dates as BC and AD, following the Church's own usage; Chapter 1 notes once that the companion books use BCE and CE for the same years.

Companion books: for the history of the councils, the East-West schism and the Reformation, point to Historical Christianity (REL 201); for Christianity among the world's religions, point to History of Religion (REL 101). Do not retell those histories here.

canon.role: The primary source for Catholic teaching in Chapters 5 to 8 and for the senses of Scripture, cited by paragraph; use the current text, including the 2018 revision of paragraph 2267.

canon.cite: Second Vatican Council. (1965). Dei Verbum: Dogmatic constitution on divine revelation. Holy See.
canon.role: The Church's teaching on revelation, Scripture, Tradition, inspiration and the formation of the Gospels (Chapters 2 and 4); promulgated by Pope Paul VI on November 18, 1965.

canon.cite: Pontifical Biblical Commission. (1993). The interpretation of the Bible in the Church. Libreria Editrice Vaticana.
canon.role: How the Church evaluates the historical-critical method and other approaches (Chapter 2); the warrant for reporting scholarship alongside teaching.

canon.cite: Confraternity of Christian Doctrine. (2011). The New American Bible, Revised Edition. Confraternity of Christian Doctrine.
canon.role: The Bible text quoted throughout, with its book introductions and notes; free to read online from the United States Conference of Catholic Bishops.

canon.cite: Brown, R. E. (1997). An introduction to the New Testament. Doubleday.
canon.role: Standard historical-critical introduction by a Catholic priest and scholar (Anchor Bible Reference Library): dating, authorship and content of each New Testament book (Chapter 4), reported as scholarship, not teaching.

canon.cite: Boadt, L. (2012). Reading the Old Testament: An introduction (2nd ed., R. J. Clifford & D. J. Harrington, Rev.). Paulist Press.
canon.role: Catholic scholarly introduction to the Old Testament, updated for archaeology and recent scholarship (Chapter 3), reported as scholarship.

bible.care: This book presents Catholic belief accurately and respectfully in the Church's own terms and sources, and it never preaches, argues the reader into faith, or argues against it. Faith claims and historical claims are kept apart: claims of faith (that Scripture is inspired, that Jesus rose from the dead, that Christ is truly present in the Eucharist) are stated as what the Church teaches and Catholics believe, with the source, and are never presented as findings of history; historical findings are never presented as proving or disproving them. Historical and critical scholarship (dating and authorship, the archaeology of the Exodus and the conquest, the synoptic question) is reported as scholarship, with the range of views and with the Church's own stance on such methods (Dei Verbum 12; Pontifical Biblical Commission, 1993). Distinguish defined dogma, ordinary teaching, theological opinion and popular devotion, and never present an opinion or a private revelation as Church teaching. Describe other Christians, Jews and people of other faiths fairly: explain the Protestant canon and the Jewish reading of the Hebrew Bible without polemic, and follow the Church's own teaching that the Jewish people are not to be blamed for Christ's death (Nostra Aetate 4). On contested moral teaching (sexuality, marriage, abortion, the end of life, the death penalty), state the teaching with Catechism references, including the 2018 revision of CCC 2267, note honestly that some Catholics and others disagree, and give no personal pastoral advice; point readers with personal questions to a priest, pastoral minister or counselor.

title: Color: Light, Vision, and the Art of Combining Colors
description: An introduction to color for artists, designers and anyone curious about why things look the way they do. The course follows color from light and the spectrum through the eye and brain, then to the systems people use to mix, specify and combine colors: additive and subtractive mixing, RGB, CMYK, HSL, CIELAB and Munsell, and the contrast studies of Itten and Albers. Later chapters cover color in art and design, accessibility for people with color vision deficiency, and how languages and cultures name colors. On-screen labs with sliders and calculators, and paper studies in the spirit of Albers, let you test every idea with your own eyes.
prerequisites: None.
For the labs and studies: a computer or phone, and colored paper, paints or colored pencils.
objectives: Explain how the color we see depends on the light source, the surface and the observer.
Describe how three cone types and opponent processing in the brain produce color vision, and use them to explain metamers, afterimages and color constancy.
Predict the results of additive mixing with light and subtractive mixing with inks and paints.
Describe a color in RGB, CMYK, HSL, CIELAB and Munsell terms, and say what each system is for.
Demonstrate simultaneous contrast and other color interactions with Albers-style studies.
Build a palette for a design and check it against the WCAG contrast rules and the common types of color vision deficiency.
Explain how languages divide up color and what research shows about color terms and meanings across cultures.

chapters.title: Light and the Spectrum
chapters.summary: What light is, how Newton's prism experiments split white light into a spectrum, and how surfaces absorb, reflect and scatter light to give objects their colors; a wavelength explorer lab fits here.
chapters.challenge: Look at sunlight, an incandescent or LED bulb and a phone screen through a prism or an inexpensive diffraction grating, sketch each spectrum, and explain why they differ.

sections.title: Light as electromagnetic radiation
sections.summary: Wavelength, frequency and the narrow band, roughly 400 to 700 nanometers, that our eyes can see.

sections.title: Newton and the spectrum
sections.summary: How prisms split and recombine white light, and why the spectrum has no sharp boundaries between colors.

sections.title: Light sources
sections.summary: Why sunlight, incandescent bulbs and LEDs have different spectra, and why the same shirt looks different under each.

sections.title: How surfaces make color
sections.summary: Absorption, reflection and scattering, from a red apple to the blue sky.

chapters.title: The Eye and Color Vision
chapters.summary: How three types of cone cells and the brain's opponent channels turn light into color, and why color is made by the observer as much as by the light; an afterimage and cone-response lab fits here.
chapters.challenge: Make a set of afterimage tests (stare at a colored shape, then look at white paper), record the colors you see, and explain each result with opponent processing.

sections.title: Rods and cones
sections.summary: The light-sensing cells of the retina, and the three cone types most sensitive to long, medium and short wavelengths.

sections.title: Trichromacy and metamers
sections.summary: The three-receptor theory of Young and Helmholtz, and how different mixtures of light can look exactly the same.

sections.title: Opponent processing
sections.summary: Hering's red-green, blue-yellow and light-dark channels, afterimages, and how the two theories fit together.

sections.title: Color constancy and context
sections.summary: How the brain discounts the color of the light, and what the 2015 dress photograph revealed about it.

chapters.title: Mixing Color: Additive and Subtractive
chapters.summary: Why red and green light make yellow while cyan and magenta inks make blue, and how screens, printers and paints each mix color; an RGB slider lab fits here.
chapters.challenge: Paint a color wheel from three paints (cyan, magenta and yellow, or a warm and a cool version of each traditional primary), then match three of its colors on screen with RGB sliders and compare the two kinds of mixing.

sections.title: Additive mixing with light
sections.summary: Red, green and blue primaries, and how a screen's tiny lights make every color it shows.

sections.title: Subtractive mixing with inks and pigments
sections.summary: How cyan, magenta and yellow each absorb part of the spectrum, and why mixtures get darker.

sections.title: Real paints
sections.summary: Why paint mixtures depart from the ideal theory, and where the traditional red, yellow and blue primaries come from.

sections.title: Halftones and pointillism
sections.summary: How printing builds colors from small dots, and what Seurat's dots do and do not do in the eye.

chapters.title: Color Models and Color Spaces
chapters.summary: The systems used to describe and measure color: RGB and CMYK for devices, HSL for picking, Munsell for artists, and CIE XYZ and CIELAB for measurement; a converter lab that shows one color in every model fits here.
chapters.challenge: Choose five colors from objects around you, match each on screen, record them in RGB, HSL and CIELAB, find the nearest Munsell notation, and compute the color difference between two of them.

sections.title: Hue, saturation and lightness
sections.summary: The three dimensions of color appearance, and the HSL and HSV models built on them.

sections.title: The Munsell system
sections.summary: Albert Munsell's hue, value and chroma, spaced by how colors look to people.

sections.title: Device color: RGB, sRGB and CMYK
sections.summary: Why the same RGB numbers can look different on two screens, and what a color profile does.

sections.title: CIE colorimetry and CIELAB
sections.summary: The 1931 standard observer, XYZ values and the chromaticity diagram, and CIELAB's attempt to space colors evenly.

chapters.title: Harmony and Contrast
chapters.summary: The classic color schemes and Itten's seven contrasts, then Albers's studies showing that one color can look like two and two colors can look like one; a simultaneous-contrast lab fits here.
chapters.challenge: Following Albers, make one color look like two different colors by placing it on two different grounds, using colored paper or a screen, then make two different colors look alike.

sections.title: Color wheels and schemes
sections.summary: Complementary, analogous, triadic and split-complementary schemes, and what a color wheel can and cannot tell you.

sections.title: Itten's seven contrasts
sections.summary: Contrasts of hue, light and dark, cold and warm, complements, simultaneous contrast, saturation and extension.

sections.title: Albers and the relativity of color
sections.summary: Exercises from Interaction of Color showing that surrounding colors change what we see.

sections.title: Do harmony rules work?
sections.summary: What experiments on color preference show, and where harmony rules are tradition rather than law.

chapters.title: Color in Art and Design
chapters.summary: How painters and designers have used color, from mineral pigments to synthetic dyes and screens, and how to build a palette that works; a grayscale-check lab fits here.
chapters.challenge: Design a five-color palette for a poster or an app screen, explain each choice with the ideas from Chapter 5, and check that it still reads when converted to grayscale.

sections.title: A short history of pigments and dyes
sections.summary: From ochre and ultramarine to Prussian blue, mauve and modern synthetic colors.

sections.title: How painters use color
sections.summary: Value, temperature and atmosphere in painting from the Impressionists onward, and what vision science says about how these effects work.

sections.title: Color in graphic and interface design
sections.summary: Palettes, hierarchy and emphasis, and why differences in lightness, more than in hue, make text and shapes easy to read.

sections.title: Color in charts and maps
sections.summary: Sequential, diverging and categorical palettes, and why rainbow color scales mislead.

chapters.title: Accessibility and Color Blindness
chapters.summary: The types and causes of color vision deficiency, which affects about 8 percent of men and under 1 percent of women of Northern European ancestry, and how to design for everyone using the WCAG contrast rules; a contrast-ratio calculator and color-blindness simulator lab fits here.
chapters.challenge: Audit a website or poster: compute the contrast ratio of its text with the WCAG formula, simulate how it looks to a viewer with deuteranopia, and redesign whatever fails.

sections.title: Types of color vision deficiency
sections.summary: Protan, deutan and tritan types, anomalous trichromacy and dichromacy, and why red-green types are by far the most common.

sections.title: Genetics and testing
sections.summary: X-linked inheritance, how prevalence varies across populations, and how Ishihara plates and anomaloscopes work.

sections.title: Contrast and WCAG
sections.summary: Relative luminance, the contrast ratio, and the minimums of 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text and for interface parts and graphics.

sections.title: Never color alone
sections.summary: Labels, patterns, shapes and position, so that no information is carried by color alone.

chapters.title: Color Names and Culture
chapters.summary: How languages divide up color, what Berlin and Kay's 1969 study and later research found, and how the meanings of colors vary across cultures and history.
chapters.challenge: List the basic color words of a language you know, or interview a speaker of another language, and compare them with the Berlin and Kay sequence.

sections.title: Basic color terms
sections.summary: Berlin and Kay's survey, the World Color Survey that followed, and the debate over universals.

sections.title: Does language change what we see?
sections.summary: Experiments on Russian speakers' two words for blue and other tests of whether words shape perception.

sections.title: Color meanings across cultures
sections.summary: White for weddings or for mourning, red for luck or for danger: which associations are widely shared and which are local.

sections.title: Naming colors precisely
sections.summary: Standard naming systems, from Munsell and ISCC-NBS to web color names and paint-chip names.

preface:
Color seems simple until you look closely. A red apple is not red in the dark. The same gray square looks lighter on a black background than on a white one. Red and green light together make yellow, but red and green paint make a muddy brown. This book explains all of that, and it starts at the beginning, with light, then the eye, then the brain, because color happens in all three.

The first half is the science: what light is, how three kinds of cone cells and the brain turn it into color, how mixing works on a screen and on paper, and how color is measured and described in numbers. The second half is the craft: how colors change each other, how artists and designers choose them, how to make sure people with color blindness can read what you make, and how languages and cultures name colors.

You will learn by doing. Most chapters have a lab on screen, with sliders that mix light or a calculator that checks contrast, and a study on paper in the spirit of Josef Albers, who taught that the way to understand color is to watch it change before your eyes. Keep your studies in one folder. By the last chapter it will hold a tested palette of your own and a small color course you made yourself.

bible.teacher: Dr. Professor teaches this book as a color scientist who also paints: physics and vision science explain what color is, and the studio exercises of Albers and Itten train the eye. Scientific claims rest on Fairchild, Berns, Livingstone and the CIE; studio methods come from Albers and Itten and are presented as artists' teaching, not as laws of nature.
bible.promise: By the last page you will explain why any color looks the way it does, mix and specify colors on screen and on paper, and choose palettes that work, read clearly and include people with color vision deficiency.
threads: Color is made in three places: the light, the object, and the observer's eye and brain.
Context changes color: the same light can look different, and different light can look the same.
Numbers and eyes together: every color model is a tool for describing what people see, and is tested against what people see.
Learn by doing: each chapter has an on-screen lab and a paper study.
Design for everyone: contrast and accessibility for color vision deficiency are part of good color, not an afterthought.

runningExamples.name: A red apple
runningExamples.use: Followed through the book: the light that falls on it (Ch 1), the cones it excites (Ch 2), how to paint or print it (Ch 3), its numbers in sRGB and CIELAB (Ch 4), and how it looks to a viewer with deuteranopia (Ch 7).

runningExamples.name: The gray square
runningExamples.use: One gray placed on different grounds, used to show simultaneous contrast (Ch 2), Albers's relativity of color (Ch 5) and the role of value in design (Ch 6).

runningExamples.name: The 2015 dress photograph
runningExamples.use: A real case of people disagreeing about a color, used for color constancy (Ch 2) and as a reminder that color is made by the observer.

runningExamples.name: Your color study folder
runningExamples.use: Screen and paper studies the reader makes chapter by chapter, ending with a palette tested for contrast and color vision deficiency (Ch 6, Ch 7).

conventions: Wavelengths in nanometers (nm); always name the model with color coordinates (sRGB 255, 0, 0; CIELAB L*, a*, b*).
American spelling (color) except in titles and quotations; write model and standard names as their standards do (CIELAB, sRGB, CIE 1931).

Keep measured facts and artistic tradition apart: Itten's and Albers's teachings are presented as influential practice, harmony rules as conventions, and claims about color and emotion with the strength of their evidence.
Use correct terms for color vision deficiency (protanopia, deuteranopia, tritanopia, anomalous trichromacy), and never imply that people with it see no color.
Each chapter names where a hands-on lab fits; labs use correct formulas, such as WCAG relative luminance and the sRGB to CIELAB conversion.

canon.cite: Albers, J. (2013). Interaction of color (50th anniversary ed.). Yale University Press.
canon.role: The studio method: exercises showing that colors change with their surroundings (Chapters 5 and 6), presented as an artist's teaching, with the perceptual explanations checked against vision science.

canon.cite: Itten, J. (1970). The elements of color (F. Birren, Ed.; E. van Hagen, Trans.). Van Nostrand Reinhold.
canon.role: Itten's color wheel and seven contrasts (Chapter 5), a condensation of his The Art of Color (1961), presented as influential Bauhaus teaching rather than scientific law.

canon.cite: Fairchild, M. D. (2013). Color appearance models (3rd ed.). John Wiley & Sons.
canon.role: The standard reference on color vision, colorimetry and color appearance: cones, opponent processing, chromatic adaptation, CIELAB and appearance effects (Chapters 2, 4 and 5).

canon.cite: Berns, R. S. (2019). Billmeyer and Saltzman's principles of color technology (4th ed.). John Wiley & Sons.
canon.role: The color science textbook for light sources, colorants and subtractive mixing, measurement, metamerism and color difference (Chapters 1, 3 and 4).

canon.cite: Livingstone, M. (2014). Vision and art: The biology of seeing (Rev. and expanded ed.). Abrams.
canon.role: How the visual system explains effects that artists use, especially luminance and equiluminance; written for general readers by a Harvard neurobiologist (Chapters 2 and 6).

canon.cite: CIE. (2018). Colorimetry (4th ed., CIE 015:2018). International Commission on Illumination. https://doi.org/10.25039/TR.015.2018
canon.role: The international standard for standard observers, illuminants, tristimulus values, chromaticity and CIELAB (Chapter 4).

canon.cite: World Wide Web Consortium. (2023). Web content accessibility guidelines (WCAG) 2.2. W3C Recommendation.
canon.role: The accessibility rules used in Chapter 7: text contrast of at least 4.5:1 (3:1 for large text), 3:1 for interface components and meaningful graphics, and color never the only means of conveying information.

bible.care: Color theory mixes science with a long artistic tradition, and the book keeps them distinct. Itten's and Albers's teachings and color-wheel harmony rules are presented as influential practice, and popular claims that particular colors reliably change mood, appetite or behavior are reported with their evidence, which is often weaker than popular accounts suggest. Color vision deficiency is described accurately and respectfully: it is common (about 8 percent of men and under 1 percent of women of Northern European ancestry, and less common in some other populations), it rarely means seeing no color at all, and designing for it is the designer's job. Color meanings in other cultures are described with sources and without stereotypes.

title: Creativity and Inspiration: Beating Writer's Block
description: A course for anyone who wants to write, or make anything, and keeps getting stuck. It starts with what psychologists have found about creativity: how ideas form, why they often arrive after a break, and why limits can help more than they hurt. It then explains why blocks happen, using Mike Rose's studies of blocked student writers and Robert Boice's studies of blocked professors, and turns that evidence into methods you can use tomorrow. Every chapter ends with a writing exercise, so you finish with a habit and a stack of pages, not just ideas.
prerequisites: None; a notebook or a document you can write in is enough
A writing project you care about, large or small (helpful but not required)
objectives: Explain divergent and convergent thinking and point to each in your own writing process.
Describe Wallas's four stages of creative work and summarize what experiments show about incubation.
Diagnose a writing block using Rose's analysis of rigid rules and plans and Boice's findings on bingeing and perfectionism.
Set up a scheduled writing routine and keep a log of minutes and words for at least four weeks.
Use freewriting, idea capture and chosen constraints to produce material on demand.
Revise a draft in separate passes for structure, paragraphs and sentences.
Tell research findings apart from practitioner advice and judge how strong each claim about inspiration is.

chapters.title: What Creativity Is
chapters.summary: The research definition of creativity, and the myths that make starting feel harder than it is.
chapters.challenge: Write 300 words about a time you made something new, then mark which parts came from effort, which from luck and which from other people.

sections.title: Novel and useful: the working definition
sections.summary: How researchers define creativity, and why both parts of the definition matter.

sections.title: Big-C, little-c and everyday creativity
sections.summary: Creativity in daily work and hobbies, not only in famous geniuses.

sections.title: The lone genius and the lightning bolt
sections.summary: What studies of real creators show about effort, drafts, collaboration and sudden inspiration.

sections.title: Creativity as something you practice
sections.summary: Why knowledge, skill and habits matter alongside personality.

chapters.title: Generating and Choosing: Divergent and Convergent Thinking
chapters.summary: Producing many options and judging among them are different kinds of thinking, and writers get stuck when they mix them up.
chapters.challenge: In ten minutes, list 30 possible titles or first lines for your project without judging any of them, then choose three and write why.

sections.title: Divergent thinking and how it is measured
sections.summary: J. P. Guilford's idea, the Alternate Uses Task, and fluency, flexibility and originality.

sections.title: Convergent thinking and judgment
sections.summary: Narrowing, choosing and evaluating ideas.

sections.title: Why mixing the two causes trouble
sections.summary: Judging each sentence as you write it, and why separating the modes helps.

sections.title: Quantity and quality
sections.summary: What research says about producing many ideas in order to find good ones.

chapters.title: The Stages of Creative Work
chapters.summary: Wallas's four stages, what experiments show about incubation, and what they mean for a writer's week.
chapters.challenge: Start a short piece today, stop after 20 minutes in the middle of a sentence, take a walk, and write for 20 more minutes tomorrow; note what changed.

sections.title: Wallas's four stages
sections.summary: Preparation, incubation, illumination and verification, from The Art of Thought (1926), and why the stages overlap.

sections.title: What incubation experiments show
sections.summary: When a break helps with a stuck problem, and what kind of break helps most.

sections.title: Insight and the aha moment

preface:
This book is for anyone who wants to write and keeps not writing. Maybe you stare at a blank page, or start strong and stall halfway, or wait for a mood that rarely comes. You are in good company, and here is the good news: being stuck has been studied. Researchers have watched blocked writers at work, counted their pages, and tested what helps.

We begin with what creativity research says: how ideas form, why the answer often turns up after you walk away, and why a limit can help you more than a blank page. Then we look at why blocks happen, through two careful studies of stuck writers: Mike Rose's work with college students and Robert Boice's work with professors. The second half turns that evidence into methods: writing on a schedule, freewriting, catching ideas, choosing constraints and revising in passes.

Pick one project in Chapter 1, anything you want to write, and bring it to every chapter. Each chapter ends with a timed writing exercise, and you will keep a small log of what you wrote. When an idea comes from research, I will tell you how strong the evidence is; when it comes from a writer's experience, I will say that too. By the end you will have a routine, a log that shows it working, and pages you did not have before.

bible.teacher: Dr. Professor teaches this book as a writing researcher who also writes every day: claims about creativity come from psychology and composition research (Sawyer and Henriksen, Rose, Boice, Silvia), practitioner advice is labeled as practitioner advice, and every idea is tried on the page in the same chapter.
bible.promise: By the last page you will know why you get stuck, have a writing routine that does not wait for inspiration, and have finished pages to show for it.
threads: Generate first, judge later: divergent and convergent thinking are different jobs.
Habits beat moods: regular scheduled writing is the best-supported answer to blocking.
Blocks have causes you can find (rigid rules, perfectionism, binge writing), so they can be fixed.
Research or practitioner wisdom: say which is which, and how strong the evidence is.
Write in every chapter: each one ends with pages, not just notes.

conventions: Label every claim's source: a study (with year and who was studied), a review, or practitioner advice.

bible.care: Present creativity research at its real strength: many findings come from lab tasks, small samples or interviews, and the book says so. Keep practitioner advice (Lamott, the tips in Silvia and Boice) labeled as such. Do not promise that any method cures every block. Chapter 5 says plainly that long-lasting inability to write together with low mood, loss of interest or anxiety that affects daily life can be depression or an anxiety disorder, and that a doctor or counselor can help. Do not repeat popular myths as fact (left-brain and right-brain creativity, the tortured genius, creativity as a fixed gift).

title: Dinosaurs: How They Lived, How They Died, and How We Know
department: Department of Earth Sciences, Paleontology Program
description: An introduction to dinosaurs for readers with no background in geology or biology. The course explains what makes an animal a dinosaur, how fossils form and how rocks are dated, the main dinosaur groups, and what bones, eggs, footprints and fossil feathers reveal about how dinosaurs grew, moved and behaved. It follows one line of small feathered dinosaurs into the birds alive today and examines the asteroid impact that ended the age of the non-avian dinosaurs 66 million years ago. Throughout, every claim is tied to the evidence and methods paleontologists use, and settled findings are kept apart from open questions.
objectives: Define a dinosaur by its anatomy and family tree, and distinguish dinosaurs from pterosaurs, marine reptiles and other prehistoric animals.

Use the Paleobiology Database to find where, and in what rocks, a dinosaur has been found.

preface:
This book is for anyone who has stood under a dinosaur skeleton and wanted to know more than its name. We begin with what a dinosaur actually is, which is more surprising than it sounds, and with how fossils form and how rocks are dated. Then we meet the big groups, look inside their bones to see how fast they grew, follow their footprints, and examine the feathered fossils that changed how we picture them. The book ends with the asteroid that struck 66 million years ago, and with the dinosaurs that survived it.

Those survivors are the birds. If you have read our Birds book (ORN 101), you have already met the American Robin as a living dinosaur; here you will see the evidence from the other side of that story. You will also keep a dinosaur file. In Chapter 1 you choose one dinosaur, and in every chapter after you add what you have learned about it, using the Paleobiology Database, the same open database scientists use.

Paleontology changes every year, as new fossils are found and old ones are studied with new tools. So each chapter separates what is settled from what is still argued, and every claim comes with the evidence behind it. By the end you will know not just what we think about dinosaurs, but how we know it.

bible.teacher: Dr. Professor teaches this book as a field paleontologist would: from fossils in the ground and in museum drawers, from rock layers and their dates, and from the lab methods (thin sections, CT scans, chemistry) that let bones answer questions.
bible.promise: By the last page you will know what a dinosaur is, how dinosaurs lived and died, why birds count as dinosaurs, and how paleontologists know all of it.
threads: How we know: every claim is tied to fossils, rocks and methods (dating, bone microstructure, trackways, CT scans, chemistry).
Birds are living dinosaurs: evolution connects the Mesozoic to the backyard (ORN 101).

bible.care: Where the science is unsettled (how the main dinosaur branches connect, how aquatic Spinosaurus was, the role of Deccan volcanism, how flight began, how warm-blooded particular dinosaurs were), present the main views with their evidence and say the question is open. title: Ethics and Metaethics: Right Action, Good Lives and the Nature of Morality
description: A course for readers who have met some moral philosophy, in an introductory class or through their own reading, and want to go deeper. The first half sets out the four main normative theories (consequentialism, deontology, virtue ethics and contractualism) at their strongest and tests each against the same small set of cases. The second half asks what morality itself is: whether there are moral facts, what moral words mean, how we could know right from wrong, and what experimental psychology has added. Each chapter ends with a written exercise in building or answering an argument.
prerequisites: An introductory course or book in philosophy or ethics, or equivalent reading
Comfort reading short primary texts and following an argument step by step
objectives: Reconstruct a moral argument as numbered premises and a conclusion, and identify which premises rest on intuitions about cases.

State the strongest objection to each normative theory and the best reply its defenders give.

Set out Mackie's arguments from relativity and from queerness and the error theory they support.
Distinguish realism, expressivism and constructivism, and explain the Frege-Geach problem.
Assess evolutionary debunking arguments and the main findings of empirical moral psychology, including their limits.
Write a short essay defending a position on one normative and one metaethical question against the best objection.

sections.summary: Kantian and Humean constructivism (Korsgaard, Street): moral truth as what correct practical reasoning would build.

chapters.title: Moral Knowledge and Moral Psychology
chapters.summary: How we could know moral truths, and what evolutionary theory and experiments say about moral judgment.
chapters.challenge: Choose one published experiment on moral judgment, summarize its method and result, and argue carefully about what it does and does not show for a philosophical theory.

sections.title: Intuitionism and coherence
sections.summary: Self-evidence, reflective equilibrium and the problem of persistent moral disagreement.

sections.title: Evolutionary debunking arguments
sections.summary: Street's Darwinian dilemma, Joyce's argument, and realist replies.

sections.title: Dual-process models and their critics
sections.summary: Greene's trolley studies, Haidt's social intuitionism, and the replication record.

sections.title: Character and situation
sections.summary: Situationist experiments, the challenge they pose to the virtue ethics of Chapter 4, and what survives it.

preface:
This book is for readers who have met moral philosophy before and want to understand it properly: not a tour of famous names, but the arguments themselves, set out carefully enough that you can test them. The first five chapters ask what we ought to do. We take the four main families of theory (consequentialism, deontology, virtue ethics and contractualism) and give each its best case before giving it its hardest objection. The last three chapters ask a stranger question: what is morality, that there could be answers at all?

We will keep coming back to a small set of cases. A runaway trolley is about to kill five people, and you can switch it onto a track where it will kill one, or, in the harder version, stop it by pushing a large man off a footbridge. You promised a dying friend to give her savings to her nephew, but the money would do far more good at a famine charity. A child is drowning in a shallow pond, and wading in will ruin your clothes. And in Gilbert Harman's example, you turn a corner and see some children setting a cat on fire. Every theory, and later every view about what morality is, has to say something about these cases, and watching each one try is the fastest way to see what it really commits you to.

I will not tell you which theory is true. I will tell you what each one says, why serious people hold it, what the best objection is, and where the evidence from psychology bears on the argument and where it does not. By the end you should be able to defend your own view against someone who knows the literature, which is the real test of having understood it.
