bible.teacher: Dr. Professor teaches this book as an analytic moral philosopher would: from the primary texts (Aristotle, Kant, Mill, Moore, Mackie) and the standard textbooks, reconstructing every position as an argument, testing it against cases and pairing it with its strongest objection; claims about moral psychology come from the published studies, with their methods and limits.
bible.promise: By the last page you will be able to state, apply and criticize the main normative theories and metaethical positions, and defend your own view on both kinds of question against a well-read opponent.
threads: Theories are tested against cases, and cases against theories: reflective equilibrium runs through every chapter.
Each view gets its strongest form before its strongest objection.
Keep three questions apart: normative (what is right?), metaethical (what is rightness?) and empirical (how do people actually judge?).
Arguments are written out as numbered premises so the reader can see exactly where to push.

runningExamples.name: The trolley family (Switch, Footbridge, Loop and Transplant)
runningExamples.use: Introduced in Chapter 1 from Foot (1967) and Thomson (1976, 1985); every normative theory is applied to it, double effect is tested on it in Chapter 3, and Greene's experiments on it are examined in Chapter 8.

runningExamples.name: The deathbed promise
runningExamples.use: A promise to a dying friend against a greater good elsewhere: the test case for consequentialism's account of promises, for Kant and Ross on duty, and for what a virtuous person would do.

runningExamples.name: Singer's drowning child
runningExamples.use: From 'Famine, Affluence, and Morality' (1972): the demandingness case in Chapter 2, revisited by each later theory and by contractualists on aggregation.

runningExamples.name: Harman's burning cat
runningExamples.use: Children setting a cat on fire, from Harman's The Nature of Morality (1977): the anchor case for the metaethics chapters, on moral observation, explanation, error theory and expressivism.

conventions: Write arguments as numbered premises and a conclusion whenever the structure matters.
Name views precisely (act versus rule consequentialism; Kantian versus Rossian deontology; naturalist versus non-naturalist realism) and define every technical term at first use.
Cite primary texts by standard reference: Aristotle by Bekker number (NE 1098a), Kant's Groundwork by Academy page (4:421), Mill by chapter of Utilitarianism.
For current statements of contested positions, the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy may be cited by entry author, title and revision date.
Report psychology studies with their design, sample and whether the result has been replicated.
Companion book: for natural law and conscience as the Catholic Church itself teaches them, point to Catholicism and the Bible (THE 101), Chapter 7, rather than restating that teaching here.

canon.cite: Rachels, J., & Rachels, S. (2023). The elements of moral philosophy (10th ed.). McGraw Hill.
canon.role: Core textbook for Chapters 1 to 5: relativism, divine command, utilitarianism, Kant, the social contract and virtue ethics, with the standard objections, at an accessible level.

canon.cite: Shafer-Landau, R. (2023). The fundamentals of ethics (6th ed.). Oxford University Press.
canon.role: Second core textbook, for well-being, the normative theories, double effect and the metaethics of error theory and realism; sets the level of rigor.

canon.cite: Miller, A. (2013). Contemporary metaethics: An introduction (2nd ed.). Polity.
canon.role: Backbone of Chapters 6 to 8: Moore, Mackie, expressivism and the Frege-Geach problem, quasi-realism, naturalist and non-naturalist realism, and fictionalism.

canon.cite: Mackie, J. L. (1977). Ethics: Inventing right and wrong. Penguin.
canon.role: Primary text for the error theory and the arguments from relativity and queerness (Chapter 7).

canon.cite: Aristotle. (2014). Nicomachean ethics (R. Crisp, Trans. & Ed.; Rev. ed.). Cambridge University Press.
canon.role: Primary text for Chapter 4: eudaimonia, the function argument, the mean and practical wisdom.

canon.cite: Kant, I. (2012). Groundwork of the metaphysics of morals (M. Gregor & J. Timmermann, Trans.; Rev. ed.). Cambridge University Press.
canon.role: Primary text for Chapter 3: the good will, duty and the formulas of the categorical imperative, with Korsgaard's introduction.

canon.cite: Mill, J. S. (1998). Utilitarianism (R. Crisp, Ed.). Oxford University Press.
canon.role: Primary text for Chapter 2, in the Oxford Philosophical Texts edition based on the 1871 text.

bible.care: Present every theory at its strongest and do not declare a winner; where professional opinion leans one way, say so with dated evidence, but keep the arguments open. Faith claims and historical claims: religion enters this book only as argument. Divine command theory and natural law are examined philosophically, religious premises are labeled as such, and claims such as God's existence are neither asserted nor denied; how a living tradition teaches its own ethics belongs to the companion religion books, and any historical claim (who held a view, when) is given with its source. Keep philosophical claims distinct from empirical ones: a study can show how people judge trolley cases but not, by itself, which judgment is correct, and studies are reported with their replication status. Sensitive applied topics (killing, euthanasia, abortion, famine relief) appear as examples of argument, with the strongest views on each side and without advocacy; thought experiments are tools for testing principles, not guides to real emergencies.

title: Food Science: The Chemistry and Physics of Cooking
department: Department of Food Science and Nutrition
description: A course for cooks who follow recipes with confidence and now want to know why they work. It explains cooking as chemistry and physics: how heat moves into food, what water, proteins, starches and fats do when they are heated, mixed and cooled, how browning makes flavor, how microbes ferment food or make it unsafe, and how we perceive flavor. Most sections come with a kitchen experiment that needs only ordinary equipment and a thermometer, and the companion book, Breakfast Cooking (CUL 101), puts the same science to work at the stove.
prerequisites: Comfortable following recipes and using basic kitchen equipment.
High-school chemistry helps (atoms, molecules, acids and bases); the essentials are reviewed where they are needed.
An instant-read digital food thermometer and a kitchen scale for the experiments.
objectives: Explain how heat reaches food by conduction, convection and radiation, and predict how pan, oven and water temperatures change cooking times.
Describe what heat, acid, salt and mixing do to proteins, starches and fats, and use that to diagnose a failed dish such as rubbery eggs, a lumpy sauce or a broken mayonnaise.
Distinguish the Maillard reaction, caramelization and enzymatic browning, and control browning with temperature, moisture and pH.
Explain how yeasts, bacteria and molds ferment foods, and why related microbes cause spoilage and illness.
Apply the USDA safe minimum internal temperatures, the danger zone and the 2-hour rule, and explain how each preservation method (cold, heat, drying, salt, sugar, acid) stops microbes.
Explain how taste, smell, texture and the trigeminal sense combine into flavor, and use that to season a dish.
Design, run and record a controlled kitchen experiment that changes one variable at a time.

chapters.title: Water and Heat
chapters.summary: Why water dominates cooking, what happens when it boils and evaporates, and the three ways heat moves into food.
chapters.challenge: Cook identical potato cubes in boiling water, in steam and in a 200°C (400°F) oven, time each until tender, and explain the order they finish in using heat transfer.

sections.title: The water molecule
sections.summary: Polarity and hydrogen bonds, and why water dissolves salt and sugar and holds so much heat.

sections.title: Boiling, simmering and evaporation
sections.summary: What a boiling point is, why it falls at high altitude, and why evaporation cools a wet surface and holds off browning.

sections.title: Conduction, convection and radiation
sections.summary: The three routes heat takes into food: from a hot pan, through moving water, oil or air, and from a glowing element or flame.

sections.title: Pans, ovens and thermometers
sections.summary: How the heat capacity and conductivity of cookware change cooking, why 100°C water cooks faster than 200°C oven air, and how to measure food temperature correctly.

chapters.title: Proteins
chapters.summary: How proteins unfold and bond together when they are heated, salted, acidified or beaten, shown in eggs, meat, fish, milk and wheat.
chapters.challenge: Using pasteurized eggs, cook eggs in water held at three different temperatures for the same time and match each texture to the egg proteins that have set.

sections.title: What a protein is
sections.summary: Chains of amino acids, how they fold, and the bonds that hold a protein in shape.

sections.title: Denaturation and coagulation
sections.summary: How heat, acid, salt and beating unfold proteins and let them link into a network, from set egg whites to cheese curds.

sections.title: Meat and fish: muscle and collagen
sections.summary: Why lean cuts toughen and dry out as they heat, while cuts rich in collagen turn tender with long, moist cooking.

sections.title: Gluten
sections.summary: How two wheat proteins form a stretchy network when flour meets water and is kneaded.

chapters.title: Carbohydrates and Starch
chapters.summary: Sugars, starches, pectins and gums: how they dissolve, crystallize, swell, thicken and go stale.
chapters.challenge: Thicken equal amounts of liquid with flour, cornstarch and potato starch, compare thickness, clarity and texture hot and again after a night in the refrigerator, and explain the results by gelatinization and retrogradation.

sections.title: Sugars
sections.summary: Glucose, fructose and sucrose: sweetness, solubility, crystals and how sugar holds on to water.

sections.title: Starch granules and gelatinization
sections.summary: Amylose and amylopectin, and how starch granules swell in hot water to thicken sauces and soften grains.

sections.title: Retrogradation and staling
sections.summary: Why bread goes stale faster in the refrigerator than on the counter, and why cooled starch gels firm up and weep.

sections.title: Pectin, gums and fiber
sections.summary: The cell-wall carbohydrates that set jam, thicken without starch and give vegetables their crunch.

chapters.title: Fats, Oils and Emulsions
chapters.summary: What fats are made of, how they behave in heat, and how emulsions such as mayonnaise and vinaigrette hold oil and water together.
chapters.challenge: Make mayonnaise with pasteurized egg yolk, break it on purpose by adding the oil too fast, rescue it, and explain each step with emulsion science.

sections.title: Triglycerides: saturated and unsaturated
sections.summary: How the shape of fatty acids explains why butter is solid and olive oil is liquid at room temperature.

sections.title: Fats in the heat
sections.summary: Frying, smoke points, and why oil breaks down when it is reused.

sections.title: Emulsions and emulsifiers
sections.summary: Droplets, lecithin and proteins, and why mayonnaise holds together while vinaigrette separates.

sections.title: Fat crystals: butter, pastry and chocolate
sections.summary: How the crystal forms of fat explain spreadable butter, flaky pastry and the snap of tempered chocolate.

chapters.title: Browning: Maillard and Caramelization
chapters.summary: The browning reactions that create the flavors of toast, seared meat and caramel, and how cooks control them.
chapters.challenge: Brown sliced onions three ways (dry pan, pan with a splash of water, and dry pan with a pinch of baking soda), then compare color, aroma, texture and time, and explain the differences.

sections.title: The Maillard reaction
sections.summary: How sugars and amino acids react under heat to make brown pigments and hundreds of aroma molecules.

sections.title: Caramelization
sections.summary: What happens when sugar is heated on its own, and how caramel differs from Maillard browning.

sections.title: Controlling browning: temperature, water and pH
sections.summary: Why a wet surface will not brown, why baking soda speeds browning, and how to get a good sear.

sections.title: Enzymatic browning
sections.summary: Why cut apples and avocados turn brown, and how acid, cold and blanching stop it.

chapters.title: Fermentation and Microbes
chapters.summary: How yeasts, bacteria and molds transform food, from bread, yogurt and sauerkraut to cheese and soy sauce, and why tested recipes keep fermentation safe.
chapters.challenge: Ferment a small batch of sauerkraut or yogurt following a tested recipe exactly, record its smell, sourness and appearance each day, and explain what the microbes are doing at each stage.

sections.title: Meet the microbes
sections.summary: Bacteria, yeasts and molds: what they eat, how fast they multiply, and what slows or stops them.

sections.title: Yeast fermentation: bread, beer and wine
sections.summary: How yeast turns sugar into carbon dioxide and alcohol, and what that does to dough and drinks.

sections.title: Lactic acid fermentation
sections.summary: How lactic acid bacteria sour yogurt, sauerkraut, kimchi and sourdough, and why the acid protects the food.

sections.title: Molds and koji
sections.summary: The molds that ripen cheese and make soy sauce and miso, and how they differ from the molds that spoil food.

chapters.title: Food Safety and Preservation
chapters.summary: What makes food unsafe and the science behind every preservation method, built on the USDA rules: keep food out of the 40 to 140°F (4 to 60°C) danger zone, refrigerate within 2 hours (1 hour above 90°F, 32°C), and cook to safe minimum internal temperatures checked with a thermometer.
chapters.challenge: Audit your own kitchen: check that the refrigerator holds 40°F (4°C) or below and the freezer 0°F (-18°C) or below, check your thermometer in ice water, and write a safety plan for one meal using the USDA safe minimum internal temperatures.

sections.title: Pathogens and how they make us sick
sections.summary: The main bacteria, viruses and toxins behind foodborne illness, and why spores and some toxins survive cooking.

sections.title: Time, temperature and the danger zone
sections.summary: Why bacteria multiply fastest between 40 and 140°F (4 and 60°C), the 2-hour rule (1 hour above 90°F, 32°C), and refrigerator and freezer temperatures.

sections.title: Cooking to safe temperatures
sections.summary: The USDA safe minimum internal temperatures: 145°F (63°C) with a 3-minute rest for whole cuts of beef, pork, veal and lamb, 160°F (71°C) for ground meats and egg dishes, and 165°F (74°C) for poultry and leftovers.

sections.title: Preservation: cold, heat, drying, salt, sugar and acid
sections.summary: How each method stops or slows microbes, explained by temperature, water activity and pH.

chapters.title: Flavor Perception
chapters.summary: How taste, smell, touch and the chemical sense combine in the brain into flavor, and how cooks use that knowledge to season.
chapters.challenge: Run a blind tasting: identify foods with your nose open and pinched shut, then test how a pinch of salt changes the bitterness of grapefruit or strong coffee, and explain both results.

sections.title: Taste: the five basic tastes
sections.summary: Sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami, their receptors, and why the tongue map is a myth.

sections.title: Smell and retronasal aroma
sections.summary: Why most of what we call flavor is smell, sensed from the back of the mouth as we chew and swallow.

sections.title: Texture, temperature and the chemical sense
sections.summary: Mouthfeel, and the trigeminal nerve that feels the burn of chili and the cool of mint.

sections.title: Balancing flavor
sections.summary: How salt, acid, sweetness, bitterness and fat change each other, and why people taste the same food differently.

preface:
This book is for cooks who can already follow a recipe and now want to know why it works. Why does a steak brown in a hot, dry pan and turn gray in a crowded one? Why does mayonnaise hold together, and why does it sometimes break? Why does bread go stale faster in the refrigerator than on the counter? Each of these questions has an answer in chemistry or physics, and the answers make you a better cook, because once you know what is happening in the pan you can fix what goes wrong.

We start with water and heat, since nearly all cooking is water being heated. Then we take the main molecules of food one at a time (proteins, carbohydrates and fats), watch what heat does to each, and see how they combine when food browns. The last three chapters turn to living things and to ourselves: the microbes that ferment food or spoil it, the rules that keep food safe, and the senses that turn chemistry into flavor.

Three foods run through the whole book: an egg, a loaf of bread and a seared steak. Between them they show nearly every reaction in these pages. Most sections end with a kitchen experiment that needs nothing more than a pan, a scale and a good thermometer. Change one thing at a time, write down what you see, and you are doing food science.

This book has a practical companion, Breakfast Cooking, which takes these ideas to the stove one morning at a time. Read them in either order; each points to the other.

bible.teacher: Dr. Professor teaches this book as a food scientist who cooks: every technique is explained by the molecules and microbes involved, and every explanation is tested with a kitchen experiment. Mechanisms come from McGee and the food science textbooks, practical tests from López-Alt, and every safety rule from USDA FSIS, quoted exactly.
bible.promise: By the last page you will look at any recipe and say what each step does to the food, predict what will happen if you change it, and keep the food safe while you experiment.
threads: Food is mostly water, and cooking is mostly moving heat into it: every chapter comes back to water and temperature.
Structure explains behavior: proteins, starches and fats act as they do because of their shapes and bonds.
One variable at a time: each chapter has an experiment with a control, a single change and a written record.
Safety is science too: USDA temperatures and times are stated exactly, with the microbiology that explains them.
From theory to the stove: chapters point to the matching cook-along in the companion book, Breakfast Cooking (CUL 101).

runningExamples.name: The egg
runningExamples.use: Proteins in their purest kitchen form: heat transfer into the shell (Ch 1), coagulation of white and yolk (Ch 2), yolk lecithin in mayonnaise (Ch 4), browned edges of a fried egg (Ch 5), Salmonella and the 160°F (71°C) rule for egg dishes (Ch 7).

runningExamples.name: A loaf of bread
runningExamples.use: Gluten (Ch 2), starch gelatinization and staling (Ch 3), crust browning (Ch 5), yeast and sourdough fermentation (Ch 6), mold spoilage (Ch 7) and the aroma of fresh bread (Ch 8).

runningExamples.name: A seared steak
runningExamples.use: Conduction and choice of pan (Ch 1), muscle proteins and collagen (Ch 2), rendered fat (Ch 4), the Maillard crust (Ch 5), and 145°F (63°C) with a 3-minute rest (Ch 7).

runningExamples.name: The kitchen notebook
runningExamples.use: The reader's record of every experiment: the question, the one variable changed, what was held constant, the result and the explanation.

conventions: Give every temperature in both °C and °F; quote USDA safety temperatures exactly as USDA states them, in °F, with the Celsius conversion in parentheses (145°F, 63°C).
Name a molecule plainly first, then technically ("the main egg-white protein, ovalbumin").
Say which explanations are well established and which are still debated by food scientists.
Never round, relax or offer shortcuts on a safety number; temperatures and times come only from current USDA FSIS guidance.
Refer back to earlier chapters by number, and to the companion book by chapter title ("see Breakfast Cooking, Chapter 1, Eggs Every Way").

canon.cite: McGee, H. (2004). On food and cooking: The science and lore of the kitchen (Completely rev. and updated ed.). Scribner.
canon.role: The central reference for the chemistry, physics and history of every ingredient and process in the book; the default source for mechanisms.

canon.cite: Vaclavik, V. A., Christian, E. W., & Campbell, T. (2021). Essentials of food science (5th ed.). Springer.
canon.role: The university food science textbook (Food Science Text Series) the course follows for structure and definitions: water, carbohydrates, proteins, fats, fermentation, food safety and preservation.

canon.cite: Damodaran, S., & Parkin, K. L. (Eds.). (2017). Fennema's food chemistry (5th ed.). CRC Press.
canon.role: The standard advanced food chemistry reference, used to check molecular detail on water, carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, browning and flavor compounds.

canon.cite: López-Alt, J. K. (2015). The food lab: Better home cooking through science. W. W. Norton.
canon.role: Practitioner cookbook by a science-trained cook: side-by-side kitchen tests and technique comparisons used as models for the experiments, with mechanisms checked against McGee and the textbooks.

canon.cite: U.S. Department of Agriculture, Food Safety and Inspection Service. (n.d.). Safe minimum internal temperature chart. https://www.fsis.usda.gov/food-safety/safe-food-handling-and-preparation/food-safety-basics/safe-temperature-chart
canon.role: The safe minimum internal temperatures quoted exactly in Chapter 7: 145°F with a 3-minute rest for whole cuts of beef, pork, veal and lamb; 160°F for ground meats and egg dishes; 165°F for poultry and leftovers.

canon.cite: U.S. Department of Agriculture, Food Safety and Inspection Service. (n.d.). "Danger zone" (40°F - 140°F). https://www.fsis.usda.gov
canon.role: The danger zone, the 2-hour rule (1 hour above 90°F), and holding hot food at 140°F or above and cold food at 40°F or below.

bible.care: Food safety is taught as fixed rules with the science behind them, never as a matter of taste. State plainly where they apply: keep perishable food out of the danger zone, 40 to 140°F (4 to 60°C); refrigerate within 2 hours, or 1 hour when it is above 90°F (32°C); keep the refrigerator at 40°F (4°C) or below and the freezer at 0°F (-18°C) or below; and cook to the USDA safe minimum internal temperatures, checked with a food thermometer: 145°F (63°C) with a 3-minute rest for whole cuts of beef, pork, veal and lamb, 160°F (71°C) for ground meats and egg dishes, and 165°F (74°C) for all poultry and for leftovers. Any experiment that uses raw or lightly cooked egg calls for pasteurized eggs, which USDA says may be used without cooking. Fermentation experiments follow a tested recipe exactly, and when in doubt, throw it out. Low-temperature cooking and home canning are explained as science (why time matters as well as temperature, why low-acid foods carry a botulism risk) but not taught as procedures; readers who want to try them are sent to current, tested USDA instructions.

title: Historical Christianity: From Jesus of Nazareth to a Global Faith
description: A history of Christianity as historians tell it, for readers who know the outline and want the evidence and the arguments. It runs from the Judaism of the Second Temple and Jesus as a historical figure through the first churches, the creeds and councils, the parting of East and West, the medieval church and the Reformations, to a faith whose center now lies in Africa, Asia and Latin America. Every chapter works from primary sources and keeps a clear line between what historical method can establish and what Christians believe by faith. It aims to be fair to Orthodox, Catholic, Protestant and other Christians alike, and to the Jews and Muslims whose histories are entwined with theirs.
prerequisites: A general knowledge of world history, or the companion History of Religion (REL 101)
Willingness to read short primary sources in translation
objectives: Explain how historians work with religious sources, and separate historical claims from faith claims in any account of Christian origins.
Describe Second Temple Judaism and summarize what historians broadly agree about Jesus of Nazareth, with the sources behind each point.
Trace how Christian scripture, creeds and church offices took shape from Paul to the Council of Chalcedon (451).
Explain the causes and stages of the estrangement between the Eastern and Western churches, and the place of the Oriental Orthodox churches and the Church of the East.
Analyze the medieval Western church's institutions, reforms and conflicts, including crusade and inquisition, from primary sources.
Compare the Lutheran, Reformed, Radical, English and Catholic Reformations in their teaching and consequences.
Describe the growth of Christianity beyond Europe since 1500 and where Christians live today, with dated figures.
Read a primary source critically: date it, place it, identify its purpose, and say what it can and cannot show.

chapters.title: Second Temple Judaism and the Historian's Craft
chapters.summary: How historians study religious history, and the Jewish world into which Jesus was born.
chapters.challenge: Read 1 Maccabees 1 and a passage of the Community Rule from the Dead Sea Scrolls, and write a short source analysis of each: author, date, purpose, and what it shows about Judaism in the last two centuries BCE.

sections.title: Historical method and faith
sections.summary: Sources, evidence and probability, and why historians set aside claims about the supernatural without denying them.

sections.title: Judea from the Persians to the Romans
sections.summary: The Second Temple, Hellenism, the Maccabean revolt and Roman rule.

sections.title: Varieties of Judaism
sections.summary: Temple and Torah; Pharisees, Sadducees and Essenes; the Dead Sea Scrolls; and the Jews of the diaspora.

sections.title: Hopes for the end of the age
sections.summary: Apocalyptic writing, messianic expectation and the kingdom of God.

chapters.title: Jesus as a Historical Figure
chapters.summary: What can be known about Jesus of Nazareth by ordinary historical methods, and what lies beyond them.
chapters.challenge: Read Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 18.63-64, and Tacitus, Annals 15.44, and write a source analysis of each: what is likely original, what may be a later addition, and what each shows about Jesus.

sections.title: The sources and how to weigh them
sections.summary: The Gospels, Paul, Josephus and Tacitus, and the criteria historians use and argue about.

sections.title: What historians broadly agree on
sections.summary: Baptism by John, a ministry in Galilee, disciples, the kingdom of God, a clash at the Temple, and crucifixion under Pontius Pilate.

sections.title: Teacher, healer, prophet
sections.summary: Jesus' message and deeds in the setting of first-century Judaism.

sections.title: The crucifixion and the Easter faith
sections.summary: Why Rome executed Jesus, and how historians treat the disciples' belief that he had been raised.

chapters.title: The First Churches
chapters.summary: From a Jewish movement in Jerusalem to communities across the Roman Empire.
chapters.challenge: Read Pliny the Younger's letter to Trajan about the Christians and the emperor's reply (Letters 10.96-97) and explain what they show about Christian worship, Roman law and persecution around 112 CE.

sections.title: Paul and the gentile mission
sections.summary: Paul's letters as our earliest evidence, and the dispute over the Jewish law and gentile converts.

sections.title: The parting of the ways
sections.summary: How, when and how slowly Christianity and Judaism became separate religions.

sections.title: Worship, leadership and women
sections.summary: Baptism and the Lord's Supper, bishops and elders, and what the evidence shows of women's roles.

sections.title: Persecution and martyrdom
sections.summary: Nero, Pliny and Trajan, Decius and Diocletian, and the honoring of the martyrs.

chapters.title: Creeds, Canon and Councils
chapters.summary: How Christians drew the boundaries of belief and scripture, and how emperors came to be involved.

preface:
This book tells the history of Christianity the way historians tell it: from evidence, with dates, and with open arguments about what the evidence means. It is for readers who know the outline (Jesus, Paul, Constantine, Luther) and want to know how we know it, what is disputed, and how a small Jewish movement in first-century Judea became the faith of more than two billion people.

We start before Christianity, in the Judaism of the Second Temple, because neither Jesus nor Paul makes sense outside it. From there we follow the first churches, the councils that defined the creeds, the parting of East and West, the medieval church, the Reformations and the modern world, and we end where most Christians now live: in Africa, Latin America and Asia. Each chapter puts a primary source in your hands (a letter, a creed, a decree) and asks you to read it as a historian would.

Three things travel with us. The first is the Nicene Creed, which we watch being made, argued over and divided over, and which is still recited in the worship of most of the world's Christians. The second is the Lord's Supper, which Christians have celebrated and disputed in every century. The third is the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem: built by Constantine, destroyed and rebuilt, and shared today by several churches under a careful arrangement, so that its stones carry much of the story.

One rule runs through every page. History can tell you what Christians believed and why, what happened and what followed from it. It cannot tell you whether God raised Jesus from the dead, and neither will this book. I will be fair to every tradition, which sometimes means telling each of them something about its past that it would rather not hear.

bible.teacher: Dr. Professor teaches this book as a historian of Christianity would, in the manner of MacCulloch, Chadwick and Pelikan: from primary sources read in context, archaeology and the best recent scholarship, neutral about the supernatural and equally fair to every Christian tradition and to Christianity's Jewish and Muslim neighbors.
bible.promise: By the last page you will be able to tell the story of Christianity from its Jewish origins to its global present, read its key documents as a historian, and explain how and why its traditions divided, without taking sides.
threads: Historical method and faith claims: what evidence can establish, and what it must leave to belief.
Unity and division: every chapter asks what held Christians together and what drove them apart.
Doctrine has a history: beliefs were argued out in particular places, languages and politics.
Christianity was never only European: the churches of Asia and Africa appear in every era, not just the last chapter.
Primary sources first: every chapter reads at least one document closely.

Do not re-teach them here.

bible.care: This is a history, not a theology, and it follows methodological neutrality: historians explain events by causes open to public evidence, so they neither affirm nor deny claims about God's action. Faith claims are reported as the beliefs of particular people, with their sources ('Paul writes that the risen Christ appeared to him'; 'the council taught that the Son is of one being with the Father'), while historical claims carry their evidence and a stated level of confidence (almost certain, probable, disputed). That Jesus existed and was crucified under Pilate is treated as the near-consensus it is among historians; the resurrection is treated as the disciples' belief, whose origins and effects historians study, not as an event history can confirm or rule out. Be fair to every tradition and to Jews and Muslims: tell Christian hostility to Jews, the crusades, inquisitions, wars of religion, and complicity in colonialism and slavery plainly, with careful numbers and ranges and without polemic, and equally refuse the caricatures one tradition has drawn of another. Where a church's own account of its history differs from historians' reconstruction (for example, on apostolic succession or a church's founding), give both and label each.

title: The History of Religion: From the First Rituals to the Modern World
description: A first course in how religions began and how they have changed, for readers with no background in religious studies. It starts with how scholars define and study religion and with the theories and prehistoric evidence about its origins, then follows the gods of the first cities, the Axial Age, the great traditions of South and East Asia and of the family of faiths that look to Abraham, and the modern story of empire, secularization and new movements. Every tradition is described accurately and even-handedly, both in its own terms and in the light of historical evidence, and the two are kept clearly apart. The book does not ask which religion is true; it asks what people have believed and done, and how we know.
prerequisites: No background in religion or history is needed
Curiosity about traditions other than your own
objectives: Explain why religion is hard to define, and use Ninian Smart's seven dimensions to describe any tradition.
Summarize the major theories of religion's origins, from Tylor and Durkheim to the cognitive science of religion, and name the kind of evidence each relies on.
Interpret the archaeological evidence for prehistoric religion, separating what was found from how it is interpreted.
Explain the idea of the Axial Age and its critics, and describe the developments in Israel, India, China and Greece that it groups together.
Outline the origins and main branches of Hindu, Buddhist, Chinese, Jewish, Christian, Islamic and Sikh traditions.
Evaluate the secularization thesis against current survey data, and describe how new religious movements arise.
For any statement about a religion, say whether it reports the tradition's own account or historians' reconstruction.

preface:
Religion is one of the oldest things humans do. People were burying their dead with care many tens of thousands of years ago, and today most of the world's eight billion people belong to a religious tradition. This book tells the story in between: how religions began, how they changed, how they spread and split, and what is happening to them now. It is for readers starting from scratch, of any faith or none.

We begin with two questions scholars still argue about: what religion is, and why humans have it at all. Then we follow the evidence forward in time, from graves and cave paintings to the temples of the first cities, the burst of new thought that scholars call the Axial Age, the traditions of India, China and Japan, the family of faiths that look back to Abraham, and finally the modern world of empires, science, secularization and new movements.

Three tools travel with us. The first is Ninian Smart's seven dimensions of religion (ritual, story, experience, ethics, doctrine, community and material things), which let you describe any tradition fairly and in the same terms. The second is a single question asked of every age: what happens when we die? The third is a handful of sacred places, from Göbekli Tepe to Jerusalem, Bodh Gaya and Mecca, that show how religion lives in particular places on the earth.

One rule: this book does not ask whether any religion is true. It asks what people believed and did, and how we know. When I tell you a tradition's own account of its beginnings, I will say so, and when I tell you what historians reconstruct, I will say that too. Both are worth knowing, and they are not the same thing.

bible.promise: By the last page you will be able to tell the story of how religions began and changed, describe any tradition fairly in Smart's seven dimensions, and tell a tradition's account of itself from the historian's account.
threads: Two accounts, kept apart: what a tradition says about itself, and what historians reconstruct from evidence.
Smart's seven dimensions as one shared lens for every tradition.
How we know: every claim is tied to its kind of evidence (bones, buildings, texts, fieldwork, surveys) and that evidence's limits.

bible.care: This book practices methodological agnosticism: it describes what people have believed and done and explains it historically, but it neither affirms nor denies that any religion's claims are true. Faith claims and historical claims are kept apart: each tradition's account of its own origins (the revelation at Sinai, the Buddha's awakening, the revelation of the Qur'an to Muhammad) is presented accurately and respectfully as that tradition's teaching, clearly labeled, and kept distinct from historians' reconstructions, which are given with their evidence and uncertainty. Theories of religion's origins explain why humans come to believe, not whether the beliefs are true; say so in both directions, so that neither believers nor skeptics take a theory as settling the question. Treat all traditions even-handedly: give comparable care to Asian, African, indigenous and Abrahamic traditions, reject the old ranking of religions from 'primitive' to 'higher', and present interpretations of prehistoric evidence as hypotheses. Contested history (religious violence, colonial missions, disputes over holy sites) is told plainly, with sources and without taking sides.

topic: Evidence-based ways to improve a life
title: Your Life, 1000× Better*: *Results May Vary. What the Evidence Says Actually Improves a Life
description: The reader asked for a textbook that makes your life 1000 times better the moment you finish it. No book can do that, and this one says so on the cover; what it can do is teach the changes with good evidence behind them and help you test them on yourself. It covers how to judge self-help claims, sleep, physical activity, relationships, habits, attention and phones, money and happiness, and purpose, using official guidelines, long-term studies and trials. Each chapter ends with a small two-week experiment you run on your own life and record.
objectives: Grade the evidence behind a self-help claim: type of study, size of effect, and whether it has been replicated.
State the adult sleep recommendation and the Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, and plan a week that meets them.

Use cues, context and friction to build one habit and weaken another, based on Wendy Wood's research.

Run, record and evaluate small experiments on your own life, and keep the changes that work.

preface:
The person who asked for this book wanted a textbook that, once finished, makes your life 1000 times better. I would love to write that book. Nobody can, and I would be fooling you if I tried, which is the one thing Dr. Professor never does. So the title keeps the joke, and the asterisk tells the truth: results vary.

Here is what I can honestly offer. A handful of changes have good evidence behind them: sleeping enough, moving your body, keeping close relationships, building habits that run without willpower, taking your attention back from your phone, spending money in ways that bring more happiness, and having a sense of purpose. None of them is magic. Each helps a little, and together they help more than any single big promise.

The first chapter teaches you to judge self-help claims, so you can check everything that follows, including me. Then each chapter ends with a two-week experiment you run on your own life, recorded in a simple daily log. By the last page you will have real data about what helps you: not 1000 times better, but better in ways you can measure and keep.

bible.teacher: Dr. Professor teaches this book as a health psychologist who reads the studies before the headlines: official guidelines and consensus statements first (HHS, AASM and SRS), then large long-term studies and trials, then popular books by researchers, always saying what kind of evidence it is and how big the effect is.
bible.promise: By the last page you will know which changes have real evidence behind them, have tested several on your own life with honest records, and be able to judge the next big self-help claim yourself.
threads: Small, steady and measured beats big promises: no single change makes a life 1000 times better, but several modest ones add up.
How strong is the evidence? Every claim is graded (guideline, trial, long-term study, correlation, anecdote) and its size stated.
Change the setting, not your willpower: cues, friction and context.
Run the experiment: every chapter ends with a two-week test on your own life.
Everything connects: sleep, movement, relationships, habits and attention affect one another.

conventions: State the kind of evidence for every claim (guideline, randomized trial, meta-analysis, long-term observational study, or anecdote) and whether the effect is small, moderate or large.
Cite guidelines by name, edition and year (Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2nd edition, 2018).
Never call a correlation a cause; say when a finding comes from following people over time rather than an experiment.
Mention findings that failed to replicate when relevant, plainly and without mockery.

bible.care: Education, not medical or mental health care. State plainly in the relevant chapters: ongoing trouble sleeping, loud snoring with daytime sleepiness, low mood lasting two weeks or more, or thoughts of self-harm call for a doctor or mental health professional (in the US, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline). Anyone with a heart condition, another chronic illness or a pregnancy should check with a clinician before starting vigorous exercise, and everyone should build up gradually, as the guidelines advise. Grade every claim honestly; present the debate on phones, social media and well-being as unsettled where it is. Avoid sources with documented accuracy problems: do not use Matthew Walker's Why We Sleep (2017), whose errors critics have documented, and cite the consensus statement and primary studies instead; do not teach power posing or ego depletion as established. Never promise outcomes; the title's 1000× is a joke and the book says so. No shaming about weight, income, relationships or screen time.

title: Mushrooms: The Hidden Life of Fungi, from Forest to Kitchen
description: An introduction to mushrooms and the fungi that make them, for readers with no background in biology. The course explains what fungi are, how mycelium grows and spreads by spores, and how mushrooms form, then teaches the identification skills mycologists use (spore prints, gills and pores, habitat) and the deadly look-alikes every beginner must know. Later chapters cover fungi in ecosystems, growing oyster and shiitake mushrooms at home, and fungi in food and medicine. The safety rule comes first and is repeated throughout: never eat a wild mushroom identified from a book, photograph or app alone; have it confirmed in person by an expert.
prerequisites: None.
For the practical work: a notebook, a hand lens, white and dark paper for spore prints, and access to a park, woodland or a store that sells several kinds of mushrooms.
objectives: Explain what fungi are and the evidence that they are more closely related to animals than to plants.
Describe the life of a mushroom-forming fungus from spore to mycelium to mushroom.
Describe a mushroom completely using the features identification depends on: cap, gills or pores, stem, ring, volva, spore print color, habitat and season.
Recognize the features of the deadly Amanitas and other dangerous species, and explain why no single feature or folk test shows that a mushroom is safe to eat.
Explain how fungi decompose wood and leaves, partner with plant roots as mycorrhizae, and form lichens with algae or cyanobacteria.
Grow oyster mushrooms at home and describe how shiitake are grown on logs and sawdust blocks.
Describe the main uses of fungi in food and medicine, including penicillin, and separate established uses from unproven claims.

chapters.title: Fungi and People
chapters.summary: Fungi in bread, beer, cheese and soy sauce, in medicine from penicillin onward, as crop diseases and human infections, and how to judge health claims about medicinal mushrooms, most of which remain unproven.

preface:
A mushroom is the part of a fungus you can see, the way an apple is the part of a tree you can pick. The rest of the fungus is a web of fine threads hidden in soil, wood or leaves, and it is doing some of the most important work on Earth: breaking down dead plants, feeding the roots of trees, and now and then pushing up a mushroom to scatter its spores. This book is about that hidden life, and about the mushrooms we find, grow, eat and fear.

We begin with what fungi are and how they live, then learn how a mushroom grows and how to look at one the way a mycologist does: spore print, gills or pores, the base of the stem, habitat and season. Then come the dangerous mushrooms and their look-alikes, the work fungi do in forests and fields, growing your own mushrooms at home, and the long story of fungi and people, from bread and cheese to penicillin.

One rule comes before everything else, and I will repeat it often: never eat a wild mushroom that you have identified from a book, a photograph or an app alone. Some of the deadliest mushrooms look quite ordinary, and by the time their poison makes you feel ill it is already damaging the liver. Learn identification for the pleasure of knowing, and if you ever want to eat what you find, have every mushroom checked in person by an expert, such as an experienced identifier at a local mycological society.

You will need a notebook, a hand lens, some paper for spore prints, and a walk outdoors after rain. Two mushrooms will follow us through the book: the oyster mushroom, which you can buy, study and grow, and the death cap, which you will learn to recognize and never eat.

bible.teacher: Dr. Professor teaches this book as a field mycologist would: from specimens, spore prints, microscopes, cultures and DNA, following Arora's field method for identification, Kendrick's textbook for biology, and Money's research on how mushrooms grow and release spores. Safety comes first in every chapter that touches eating.
bible.promise: By the last page you will understand how fungi live, describe any mushroom with the features experts use, recognize the deadly Amanitas, grow your own oyster mushrooms, and know exactly why a book, photograph or app is never enough to eat a wild mushroom.
threads: The mushroom is the fruit; the fungus is the hidden mycelium.
Safety first: identification is taught for knowledge, and eating any wild mushroom requires in-person confirmation by an expert.
Observe completely: the whole mushroom with its base, the spore print, the habitat and the season.
How we know: claims are tied to specimens, experiments and DNA, and unproven claims are labeled unproven.
Fungi connect living things: decomposition, plant partnerships, food and medicine.

conventions: Give the scientific name in italics with the common name at a species' first mention in a chapter; common names vary by region, so the scientific name is the reference.
Never call a wild mushroom safe to eat on the strength of described features; every edible species is shown alongside its dangerous look-alikes and the in-person expert rule.
Label claims by strength of evidence (established, under study, or unproven); a health claim is called established only when human clinical trials support it.

bible.care: Wild mushrooms can kill, and the book says so plainly and often. The rule: never eat a wild mushroom identified from a book, a photograph, an app or this course alone; every mushroom meant for eating must be confirmed in person, specimen in hand, by an experienced expert such as an identifier at a local mycological society, and when in doubt, throw it out. No folk test (peeling, silver, color, smell, pleasant taste, or animals eating it) shows that a mushroom is safe. Death caps and destroying angels look ordinary, and their amatoxins cause symptoms only many hours after the meal, by which time the liver is already being damaged; anyone who may have eaten a poisonous mushroom needs emergency medical help at once, with a sample of the mushroom if possible, even if they feel well. Keep wild mushrooms away from children and pets. Cook edible mushrooms before eating them; some edible species, such as morels and shiitake, can cause illness or skin reactions when eaten raw or undercooked. Cultivation covers only known edible species (oyster, shiitake and similar) grown from reputable spawn suppliers; the book does not teach the cultivation or use of psychoactive species, which are illegal in many places. Health claims for medicinal mushrooms, and popular claims (including some from well-known mushroom advocates) about fungi curing disease, improving memory or forming forest-wide 'brains', are reported as unproven unless human clinical trials or strong field evidence support them; the 'wood wide web' is taught with its real, mixed evidence, including recent reviews that found the field evidence for trees sharing resources through fungal networks weaker than often claimed.

title: Particle Physics: The Standard Model and Its Open Questions
description: An upper-division course in particle physics for readers who have completed quantum mechanics (PHY 331 or equivalent). It follows the standard texts, Griffiths' Introduction to Elementary Particles, Thomson's Modern Particle Physics, and Halzen and Martin's Quarks and Leptons, and takes every measured value from the Particle Data Group's Review of Particle Physics. Starting from relativistic kinematics and symmetry, it builds quantum electrodynamics, quantum chromodynamics and the electroweak theory, then the Higgs mechanism and neutrino oscillation, always computing a number and comparing it with experiment. The final chapter treats what the Standard Model leaves unexplained, including the hierarchy (fine-tuning) problem and the cosmological constant problem, honestly as open questions.
prerequisites: Quantum mechanics at the level of PHY 331 (Griffiths and Schroeter): spin, addition of angular momenta, perturbation theory and Fermi's Golden Rule

preface:
On 4 July 2012, two experiments at CERN, ATLAS and CMS, announced a new particle with a mass of about 125 GeV. It had been predicted in 1964 as a consequence of an idea about how force-carrying particles can have mass. This book is about how predictions like that one are made, how they are tested, and how physicists decide that a small bump in a plot is real.

It is written for readers who have finished an upper-division course in quantum mechanics; our companion book, PHY 331, is the natural place to start. We follow the standard texts: Griffiths' Introduction to Elementary Particles for the pace, Thomson's Modern Particle Physics for the modern experiments, and Halzen and Martin's Quarks and Leptons where a calculation deserves to be done in full. Every measured number, whether a mass, a lifetime or a mixing angle, comes from the Particle Data Group's Review of Particle Physics with its uncertainty, because a value without an error bar is not a measurement.

The method is the same in every chapter: find the symmetry, turn it into Feynman rules, calculate a number, and compare it with what a detector saw. Four results keep returning. The 125 GeV Higgs boson first appears as an invariant-mass peak in Chapter 1. Electron-positron annihilation is the cleanest laboratory we have for QED, for quarks and gluons, and for the Z boson. The muon takes us from time dilation in cosmic rays to the strength of the weak force. Neutrino oscillation, established by Super-Kamiokande in 1998, was the first clear sign that the Standard Model as first written is incomplete.

The last chapter is about what we do not know. The Standard Model does not explain dark matter, the excess of matter over antimatter, or why the Higgs boson is as light as it is, and simple estimates of the energy of empty space disagree with observation by an enormous factor. These are the fine-tuning problems. I will tell you exactly what each one is, what has been proposed, what the LHC has and has not found, and where careful physicists disagree.

bible.teacher: Dr. Professor teaches this book as a particle physicist who has worked through the calculations and also read the event displays: each force is introduced by its symmetry, turned into Feynman rules, computed to a number, and checked against a measured value from the Review of Particle Physics. Griffiths sets the level and pace, Thomson supplies the modern experiments and their data, and Halzen and Martin supply the fuller calculations; the discovery papers are read as primary sources.
bible.promise: By the last page you will compute decay rates and cross sections from Feynman rules, read a discovery plot and judge its significance, explain how the Higgs mechanism and neutrino oscillation work, and state precisely what the Standard Model does not explain.
threads: Symmetry decides the forces: each interaction comes from a gauge symmetry, and a broken symmetry explains mass.
Calculate, then compare: every diagram becomes a number that a detector can check.
How we know: every measured value comes from the Review of Particle Physics with its uncertainty, and every discovery is tied to the experiment and the data that made it.
The Standard Model is extraordinarily successful and known to be incomplete; we say exactly where it fails and where it only seems unnatural.
Built on quantum mechanics (PHY 331): spin, angular momentum, two-state systems, perturbation theory and identical particles are used, not re-taught.

runningExamples.use: An invariant-mass peak in Chapter 1, made mostly by gluon fusion in Chapter 4, the consequence of symmetry breaking and the subject of Chapter 6, and the center of the hierarchy problem in Chapter 8.

runningExamples.name: Electron-positron annihilation
runningExamples.use: The cleanest laboratory: kinematics in Chapter 1, the first full QED calculation in Chapter 3, the R ratio and jets in Chapter 4, and the Z lineshape at LEP in Chapter 5.

runningExamples.name: The muon
runningExamples.use: Time dilation of cosmic-ray muons in Chapter 1, lepton number in Chapter 2, g - 2 in Chapter 3, the Fermi constant from its lifetime in Chapter 5, and muon-neutrino disappearance in Chapter 7.

runningExamples.name: Neutrino oscillation (Super-Kamiokande, 1998)
runningExamples.use: Left-handed neutrinos and helicity in Chapters 3 and 5, a two-state quantum system (PHY 331 Chapter 3) over thousands of kilometers in Chapter 7, and the open question of where neutrino mass comes from in Chapter 8.

conventions: Natural units (ħ = c = 1) from Chapter 1 onward; convert final answers to SI units with ħc = 197.3 MeV fm and show the conversion.

Every measured value (masses, widths, lifetimes, couplings, mixing parameters) comes from the 2026 Review of Particle Physics, quoted with its uncertainty and the listing it comes from; never quote a measured value from memory or a secondary source. If a value is taken from the 2024 edition, say so.
Metric signature (+, -, -, -) and Griffiths' notation; state it when Thomson or Halzen and Martin use a different normalization or convention.
Feynman diagrams are drawn with time running from left to right, and the caption says so.
Report significances as local or global, and use the experiments' own language: 'evidence' at three sigma, 'observation' at five sigma.
Label speculative ideas (supersymmetry, extra dimensions, the multiverse) as proposals, with their experimental status and the date of that status.
Refer back to PHY 331 by chapter when using quantum mechanics (for example, Fermi's Golden Rule, PHY 331 Chapter 7).

bible.care: Chapter 8 deals with open problems; keep measurement, theory and speculation clearly apart. The hierarchy (naturalness, fine-tuning) problem and the cosmological constant problem are genuine open questions: state what is measured (the Higgs mass, the dark energy density), what is a theoretical expectation and on what assumptions it rests, and why physicists disagree about whether naturalness is a reliable guide. Do not claim that the LHC has disproved supersymmetry or that naturalness proves new physics must exist; report the excluded mass ranges as the experiments state them, with dates. 'Fine-tuning' here is a technical term about sensitive cancellations in a theory; it is not, by itself, an argument for design or for a multiverse. Present anthropic reasoning as one proposal that physicists debate, fairly and without endorsing or mocking it. Mention the nickname 'God particle' only to explain where it came from and why physicists avoid it.

title: How to Get Rich (Slowly, and for Real): What the Evidence Says About Building Wealth
description: The reader asked how to get rich; this course answers with what the evidence supports. It covers the things that reliably build wealth over a lifetime: earning more through skills and career choices, spending less than you earn, letting compound growth work for decades, avoiding expensive debt, and owning low-cost diversified index funds instead of trying to pick winners. It also looks squarely at the get-rich stories (stock tips, trading, crypto, startup fortunes), how often they work out, and how to spot scams. Examples use US accounts and tax rules, and the course is education, not personal financial advice.

No finance background needed

Build a monthly budget with a savings target and an emergency fund goal.

Explain, using SPIVA data and cost arithmetic, why most actively managed funds trail their benchmark index over long periods.
Describe risk, diversification and asset allocation, and choose a stock and bond mix for a goal and time horizon.
Explain how US tax-advantaged accounts (401(k), traditional and Roth IRA, HSA) work, using the current year's IRS limits.
Identify investment fraud warning signs and survivorship bias in success stories.

preface:
You asked how to get rich. Here is the honest answer, and it is better news than it sounds: most people who build real wealth do it in ordinary ways that you can copy. They earn a decent income and grow it, spend less than they earn, avoid expensive debt, and put the difference into low-cost, diversified investments for a long time. Nothing on that list needs luck, a secret or a guru.

What this book will not do is promise you a shortcut. We will look closely at the shortcuts people sell (stock tips, day trading, the next coin, the dropout founder) and ask the question their stories skip: out of everyone who tried, how many won? Some did, and we will say how. We will also learn to recognize the scams that dress up as shortcuts.

Each chapter does the math with you. You will follow three savers who start at different ages and watch what time, fees and debt do to them, and you can move the sliders yourself in the compound-growth explorer. The examples use US accounts and taxes, and every rule that changes each year comes with its date. This is education, not advice about your own money; by the end you will know enough to make your own decisions, and to know when to ask a professional.

title: Quantum Mechanics: From Atomic Spectra to Entanglement
description: An upper-division course in quantum mechanics for readers with calculus, linear algebra and introductory physics. It follows Griffiths and Schroeter's Introduction to Quantum Mechanics (3rd ed.), with Shankar, Sakurai and Napolitano, and the Feynman Lectures Volume III as companions, and introduces every idea through the experiment that forced it. Readers solve the Schrödinger equation, work in Dirac notation, derive the hydrogen spectrum, handle spin and identical particles, and use approximation methods on real atoms. The last chapter covers entanglement and the Bell tests recognized by the 2022 Nobel Prize, presents the interpretations of quantum mechanics as an open debate, and prepares the reader for PHY 341, Particle Physics.
prerequisites: Calculus through ordinary and partial differential equations (separation of variables)
Linear algebra: complex vectors, matrices, eigenvalues and eigenvectors
Introductory classical mechanics, waves, and electricity and magnetism
A modern physics survey is helpful but not required
objectives: Explain, with numbers, how blackbody radiation, the photoelectric effect, atomic spectra and electron diffraction forced quantum theory.
Use Dirac notation, Hermitian operators and commutators to compute measurement probabilities, expectation values and uncertainty relations.
Solve the Schrödinger equation for the standard one-dimensional potentials and interpret bound states, scattering and tunneling.
Derive the energy levels of hydrogen and predict its spectral lines to within the accuracy of the model.
Describe spin one-half with Pauli matrices, predict the outcomes of Stern-Gerlach sequences, add angular momenta, and apply the Pauli principle.
Apply perturbation theory and the variational principle to fine structure, the Zeeman effect, helium and atomic transitions.
Derive the CHSH form of Bell's inequality, compute the quantum prediction, and evaluate what a published Bell test does and does not establish.
Compare the main interpretations of quantum mechanics and say which questions experiments have settled and which remain open.

chapters.title: The Experimental Crisis
chapters.summary: The measurements made between 1900 and 1927 that classical physics could not explain, and the quantum ideas they forced on physicists.
chapters.challenge: From the measured wavelengths of the first four Balmer lines of hydrogen, find the Rydberg constant, then show where the Bohr model succeeds and name two facts it cannot explain.

sections.title: Blackbody radiation and Planck's quantum
sections.summary: The ultraviolet catastrophe, Planck's 1900 fit, and energy in steps of hν.

sections.title: Light as particles: the photoelectric and Compton effects
sections.summary: Einstein's photons and Compton's X-ray scattering, with the numbers that convinced physicists.

sections.title: Atomic spectra and the Bohr model
sections.summary: The sharp lines of hydrogen, Bohr's quantized orbits, and where the model breaks.

sections.title: Matter as waves
sections.summary: De Broglie's wavelength, the Davisson-Germer experiment, and the double slit one particle at a time.

chapters.title: Wave Functions and the Schrödinger Equation
chapters.summary: The wave function, Born's rule and the Schrödinger equation, solved first for a particle confined in a box.
chapters.challenge: For a particle in an infinite square well prepared in an equal superposition of its two lowest states, compute ⟨x⟩ as a function of time, find the period of its oscillation, and check the uncertainty principle at t = 0.

sections.title: The wave function and Born's rule
sections.summary: Probability densities, normalization, and the double slit read as a probability pattern.

sections.title: The Schrödinger equation and stationary states
sections.summary: Separation of variables, energy eigenstates, and how superpositions change in time.

sections.title: The infinite square well
sections.summary: The first solved problem: quantized energies, orthogonality and completeness.

sections.title: Momentum, expectation values and uncertainty
sections.summary: Operators for observables, Ehrenfest's theorem, and the Heisenberg uncertainty principle.

chapters.title: The Formalism: Hilbert Space and Dirac Notation
chapters.summary: States as vectors, observables as operators, and the rules that turn them into predictions, illustrated on the Stern-Gerlach two-state system.
chapters.challenge: Write the state of a spin one-half particle as a ket, compute the probabilities for a Stern-Gerlach measurement along an axis tilted by an angle θ, and verify the generalized uncertainty relation for two noncommuting spin components.

sections.title: State vectors, bras and kets
sections.summary: Hilbert space, inner products, and changing basis.

sections.title: Observables and Hermitian operators
sections.summary: Eigenvalues as the possible results, eigenvectors, and completeness.

sections.title: The measurement postulates
sections.summary: Born's rule in general form and the projection postulate, stated as rules of the theory and revisited in Chapter 8.

sections.title: Time evolution and the generalized uncertainty principle
sections.summary: Unitary evolution, commutators, conserved quantities, and the energy-time relation.

chapters.title: Potentials in One Dimension
chapters.summary: The harmonic oscillator, the free particle, bound states and tunneling, solved with the tools of Chapter 3.
chapters.challenge: Compute the transmission probability through a rectangular barrier and use it to explain why the current in a scanning tunneling microscope changes by roughly a factor of ten when the tip moves 0.1 nanometer.

sections.title: The harmonic oscillator and ladder operators
sections.summary: Energy levels from raising and lowering operators, and the vibrations of real molecules.

sections.title: The free particle and wave packets
sections.summary: Plane waves, group velocity, and why a wave packet spreads.

sections.title: Bound states in wells
sections.summary: The delta-function well and the finite square well, and how many bound states fit.

sections.title: Scattering and tunneling
sections.summary: Reflection and transmission, alpha decay, and the scanning tunneling microscope.

chapters.title: Angular Momentum and the Hydrogen Atom
chapters.summary: The Schrödinger equation in three dimensions, quantized angular momentum, and the hydrogen spectrum derived from first principles.
chapters.challenge: Predict the wavelengths of the first four Balmer lines from the energy levels you derived, compare them with the NIST Atomic Spectra Database, and explain the remaining differences (reduced mass, air versus vacuum wavelengths, fine structure).

sections.title: The Schrödinger equation in three dimensions
sections.summary: Separation in spherical coordinates and the radial equation.

sections.title: Orbital angular momentum
sections.summary: Commutation relations, ladder operators, and spherical harmonics.

sections.title: The hydrogen atom
sections.summary: Energy levels, degeneracy, and the shapes of the wave functions.

sections.title: The hydrogen spectrum explained
sections.summary: The Lyman, Balmer and Paschen series, and why Bohr's energies came out right.

chapters.title: Spin and Identical Particles
chapters.summary: Spin one-half from the Stern-Gerlach experiment, the addition of angular momenta, and the symmetry rules that build the periodic table.
chapters.challenge: Predict the beam intensities after three Stern-Gerlach magnets oriented along z, then x, then z, and explain why the third magnet splits the beam again.

sections.title: The Stern-Gerlach experiment
sections.summary: Silver atoms in a nonuniform magnetic field (Frankfurt, 1922), and why the result was understood as spin only after 1925.

sections.title: Spin one-half as a two-state system
sections.summary: Spinors, Pauli matrices, sequential measurements, and spin precession in a magnetic field.

sections.title: Adding angular momenta
sections.summary: Singlet and triplet states, and Clebsch-Gordan coefficients.

sections.title: Identical particles
sections.summary: Bosons and fermions, the Pauli exclusion principle, helium, and the structure of the periodic table.

chapters.title: Approximation Methods
chapters.summary: Perturbation theory and the variational principle, used to explain the fine details of real atoms and how they absorb and emit light.
chapters.challenge: Use the variational method with an effective nuclear charge to estimate the ground-state energy of helium, compare it with the measured value, and explain why your estimate must lie above it.

sections.title: Time-independent perturbation theory
sections.summary: First- and second-order corrections, and what changes when levels are degenerate.

sections.title: Fine structure and the Zeeman effect
sections.summary: Relativistic and spin-orbit corrections to hydrogen, and atoms in magnetic fields.

sections.title: The variational principle
sections.summary: Upper bounds on ground-state energies, applied to helium.

sections.title: Time-dependent perturbation theory
sections.summary: Transitions, selection rules, spontaneous emission, and Fermi's Golden Rule.

chapters.title: Measurement, Entanglement and Bell Tests
chapters.summary: Entanglement, Bell's theorem and the experiments that tested it, ending with the measurement problem presented as an open debate.
chapters.challenge: Compute the quantum prediction for the CHSH quantity S at the optimal analyzer angles, compare it with the 2015 Delft result S = 2.42 ± 0.20, and state precisely what that result rules out and what it leaves open.

sections.title: Entanglement and the EPR argument
sections.summary: Einstein, Podolsky and Rosen's 1935 challenge, and the spin singlet as the cleanest example.

sections.title: Bell's theorem
sections.summary: Local hidden variables, the CHSH inequality, the quantum violation, and why entanglement cannot send signals.

sections.title: Testing Bell: from Clauser and Aspect to loophole-free tests
sections.summary: Experiments from 1972 to 2015, the loopholes each one closed, and the 2022 Nobel Prize.

sections.title: The measurement problem and its interpretations
sections.summary: Decoherence, Copenhagen, many worlds, pilot waves, collapse models and QBism, each in its own terms, as an open debate.

preface:
In 1922, in a laboratory in Frankfurt, Otto Stern and Walther Gerlach sent a beam of silver atoms through a magnet and found the silver deposited on a glass plate in two separate traces. Classical physics predicted one smeared band. Results like that one, which would not go away however carefully they were repeated, are where this book begins, because quantum mechanics was not invented for its elegance. Experiments forced it on physicists who did not want it.

This book is for readers who know calculus, some linear algebra and introductory physics, and who want to do quantum mechanics, not only read about it. It follows Griffiths and Schroeter's Introduction to Quantum Mechanics, the standard upper-division text, and borrows from Shankar, from Sakurai and Napolitano, and from Feynman's Lectures wherever they explain something better. Every chapter works the same way: a measurement raises a question, the mathematics answers it, and the answer is checked against a number someone actually measured.

Four experiments will keep coming back. The hydrogen spectrum is our first puzzle in Chapter 1 and our first great success in Chapter 5. The Stern-Gerlach magnet is the cleanest quantum measurement there is, and we use it to learn the formalism and then spin. The double slit, run one particle at a time, shows what a probability amplitude is. Pairs of entangled particles, first photons and then electron spins 1.3 kilometers apart, carry us to the Bell tests honored by the 2022 Nobel Prize.

The last chapter ends where physicists still argue: what a measurement is, and what the wave function describes. I will show you exactly what experiments have settled, set out the main interpretations fairly, and leave the open question open. If you go on to particle physics (PHY 341), everything here, from spin and angular momentum to perturbation theory and identical particles, is used from its first pages.

bible.teacher: Dr. Professor teaches this book as a physicist who works at the blackboard and in the lab: each idea is introduced by the experiment that forced it, built into the formalism of Griffiths and Schroeter, and then tested against a measured number. Feynman's Volume III supplies the two-state-system viewpoint and the physical intuition; Shankar and Sakurai and Napolitano supply rigor and the deeper formal treatment where the reader is ready for it.
bible.promise: By the last page you will set up and solve the Schrödinger equation for real systems, use Dirac notation and approximation methods fluently, predict the hydrogen spectrum and any Stern-Gerlach sequence, and explain exactly what Bell tests prove and what they leave open.
threads: Experiment first: every postulate is introduced by the measurement that forced it, with the place, year and numbers.
One formalism: states are vectors, observables are operators, probabilities are squared amplitudes; every chapter is that idea at work.
Exact solutions are rare; approximation and order-of-magnitude estimates are the working physicist's main tools.
Keep three things apart: what is measured, what the theory predicts, and what an interpretation adds.
This book is the foundation for PHY 341 (Particle Physics): spin, angular momentum, two-state systems, perturbation theory and identical particles all return there.

runningExamples.use: The Chapter 1 puzzle (Balmer lines and the Bohr model), solved exactly in Chapter 5, refined by fine structure and the Zeeman effect in Chapter 7, and the doorway to quantum electrodynamics (the Lamb shift) in PHY 341.

runningExamples.use: The model quantum measurement: the two-state system that teaches the formalism in Chapter 3, spin one-half and sequential measurements in Chapter 6, and spin measurements in Bell tests in Chapter 8.

runningExamples.name: The double slit, one particle at a time
runningExamples.use: An interference pattern built from single detections: wave-particle duality in Chapter 1, Born's rule in Chapter 2, superposition in Chapter 3, and which-path information and decoherence in Chapter 8.

runningExamples.name: Entangled pairs: Clauser's and Aspect's photons, and the Delft electron spins
runningExamples.use: Photon polarization as a two-state system in Chapter 3, the spin singlet in Chapter 6, and the Bell tests from 1972 to the 2015 loophole-free experiments and the 2022 Nobel Prize in Chapter 8.

conventions: Follow Griffiths and Schroeter's notation: Ψ(x, t) for the full wave function, ψ(x) for stationary states, ħ kept explicit; Dirac notation from Chapter 3 onward.

SI units, with electron volts for atomic energies and nanometers for wavelengths; physical constants from the current CODATA recommended values (NIST) and spectral lines from the NIST Atomic Spectra Database, with the source named.
Name the experimenters, place and year at an experiment's first mention in a chapter (for example, Stern and Gerlach, Frankfurt, 1922).
Label every claim as measurement, prediction or interpretation when the difference matters; no interpretation is presented as established fact.
"Observer" and "measurement" mean a physical interaction that leaves a record; never suggest that consciousness is required.
Show each worked calculation step by step with units, then check the answer by an order-of-magnitude estimate or a limiting case.
Point forward to PHY 341 by chapter where an idea returns in particle physics (for example, Fermi's Golden Rule, or neutrino oscillation as a two-state system).

canon.role: The main text: level, pace, notation and the order of topics; most worked examples and challenges are modeled on its problems.

canon.role: Companion for the mathematical formalism (Chapter 3): Hilbert space, Dirac notation and operators, developed more fully than in Griffiths and Schroeter.

canon.role: Graduate-level companion: Stern-Gerlach as the entry to the formalism, angular momentum, and the deeper treatment of symmetry, for readers who want more.

canon.role: Physical intuition: amplitudes, the double slit and two-state systems (first published 1965); used for explanations, not for notation.

canon.role: Primary source for Chapter 8: the Delft event-ready Bell test (CHSH value S = 2.42 ± 0.20) that closed the detection and locality loopholes in one experiment.

bible.care: Quantum mechanics is widely misused in popular culture ("quantum healing", claims that consciousness creates reality). State plainly, where relevant, that measurement in standard physics does not require a conscious observer, that entanglement cannot be used to send signals faster than light (the no-signaling theorem), and that the uncertainty principle is a property of quantum states, not of clumsy instruments. The interpretation of quantum mechanics is a genuine open debate among physicists and philosophers: present Copenhagen, many worlds, Bohmian (pilot-wave) mechanics, objective-collapse models and QBism fairly, each in its own terms and with its strongest case, note that the standard versions agree on all experiments done so far while collapse models are testable in principle, and do not declare a winner.

title: ROM Corrupting: Bytes, Glitches and the Art of Breaking Games
department: Department of Digital Media and Art
description: A short, hands-on course for curious players who have seen corrupted games online and want to know what is happening inside. It explains what a ROM is, how bytes and hexadecimal work, and how NES and SNES-era games store their code, graphics and data, so that every glitch you make has a cause you can name. You then use corruption tools, from simple byte changers to the Real-Time Corruptor, and look at glitch art as a serious art form. It uses only ROMs you dumped from cartridges you own, or homebrew and public-domain games, never pirated copies.
prerequisites: Comfort using a computer: installing a program and finding a file
No programming required
objectives: Explain what a ROM and a ROM image are, and how a cartridge is dumped legally.
Convert numbers between binary, decimal and hexadecimal, and read a file's header in a hex editor.
Describe how NES and SNES-era games separate code, graphics and data, and predict what corrupting each will do.
Make controlled corruptions with a byte-changing tool and with the Real-Time Corruptor, recording settings so others can reproduce them.
Discuss glitch art as an art practice using Rosa Menkman's ideas.
Share a corruption legally as a video, images or a patch, never as a ROM.

sections.summary: A 6502-based processor, a separate picture processor, and very little RAM.

chapters.summary: What corruption does at the byte level, and how to use a file corruptor and the Real-Time Corruptor.
chapters.challenge: Make five corruptions of the same homebrew game with different settings, log each setting, and choose the most interesting result.

sections.summary: Bit flips, adding to a byte, random replacement and shifting bytes.
